What is cancer?
Normally, our bodies have signals that tell cells when to stop growing, but cancer cells ignore these signals. They keep multiplying and can form lumps called tumors in different parts of the body or they replace the healthy cells in bone marrow and blood.
These cells can directly spread into, or invade, surrounding tissues, spread to lymph nodes, or spread to other organs in the body, like the lung.

What is the most common type of head and neck cancer?
The most common type of head and neck cancer is mucosal squamous cell carcinoma. This cancer begins in squamous cells, which are tiny ﬂat cells that cover and protect your mouth, throat, and voicebox.
It is important to know that squamous cells also cover many other parts of you body, like your skin and lungs. If cancer starts from these cells, this is not considered head and neck cancer.

Salivary gland carcinomas are the other major type of head and neck cancer. These can start in any of the 3 major pairs salivary glands, which make saliva and release it into the mouth.
Salivary gland cancers can also start from minor salivary glands, which line your mouth, throat, and voicebox.

Cancer Staging
Once a diagnosis is made, your doctors will need to determine:
• The size and location of the tumor
• The extent of local tissue invasion
• Whether lymph nodes are involved
• Whether the cancer has spread (metastasized) to other sites This process is called staging.
01-03-07.heading: Cancer Staging

chunks:
Cancer Staging
The following are some commonly used imaging tests. Each test has unique advantages over other tests.
• Ultrasound
• CT scan
• MRI
• PET-CT Your oncology team will choose the best test or tests for you.
01-03-08.heading: Cancer Staging

chunks:
What does the cancer stage mean?
Staging follows the TNM classiﬁcation system:
• T (Tumor): How big is the tumor? Where is it?
• N (Nodes): Has it spread to lymph nodes?
• M (Metastasis): Has it spread to other parts of the body?
01-03-09.heading: What does the cancer stage mean?

chunks:
What does the cancer stage mean?
Based on the TNM ﬁndings, the cancer is then assigned an overall stage:
• Stage 1-2: Early stage - Usually smaller tumors, may not have spread.
• Stage 3-4: Advanced stage - Usually larger, there may be nodal involvement or distant metastases.
01-03-10.heading: What does the cancer stage mean?

chunks:
Staging is Important because it Guides Treatment Strategy
Early stages (1-2) may only require one type of treatment (e.g., surgery or radiation alone). Advanced stages (3-4) usually require more than one type of cancer treatment (e.g., surgery followed by radiation or radiation with chemotherapy).
Refer to module 4 for more information about surgery and module 9 for radiation.
01-03-11.heading: Staging is Important because it Guides Treatment Strategy

chunks:
Staging is Important because it Helps Predict Prognosis
Early-stage cancers tend to have higher remission rates. Advanced-stage cancers may have a less favorable outlook, but prognosis varies based on several factors. Ask your oncology team about your prognosis.
01-03-12.heading: Staging is Important because it Helps Predict Prognosis

02-01-02.heading: Curative Head and Neck Cancer Treatments: Overview

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Treatments Aimed at Cure
The main goal of curative treatment is to eliminate the cancer and prevent it from coming back. Surgery and radiation are the two types of treatment that are known to cure head and neck cancers. Depending on the stage, location, and overall health of the patient, different combinations of treatments may be used.
02-01-03.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Treatments Aimed at Cure

chunks:
Surgery
Surgery is one of the main treatment approaches for head and neck cancers. It can treat cancers involving the mouth, throat, voice box, nose or sinonasal cavities, and saliva glands. It is rarely used to treat cancers of the throat behind the nose (nasopharynx).
Surgery is often the preferred treatment option for cancers involving the mouth, or oral cavity, and the saliva glands.
02-01-04.heading: Surgery

chunks:
Surgery
Depending on the risk of recurrence, patients may need radiation and/or chemotherapy after surgery. The risk of recurrence depends on the features and behavior of the tumor. Oftentimes, these are only fully understood after the tumor is removed.
We discuss this topic in depth in Module 9, which is titled “Postoperative Radiation and Chemotherapy.”
02-01-05.heading: Surgery

chunks:
Radiation
Radiation is the other major treatment for head and neck cancers.

Like surgery, it can treat cancers involving the front of mouth, throat, voice box, nose or sinonasal cavities, and saliva glands. It is not commonly used as the ﬁrst step of treatment for cancers involving the front of mouth, or oral cavity, and saliva glands.
02-01-06.heading: Radiation

chunks:
Radiation
Radiation is often preferred for cancers involving the back of the throat behind the mouth, or oropharynx, the back of the throat behind the nose, or nasopharynx, and voice box, or larynx.
It is also commonly used for cancers that are very large, difﬁcult to access, or where surgery may cause meaningful loss of function, such as a reduced ability to speak or swallow.
02-01-07.heading: Radiation

chunks:
Chemotherapy
Chemotherapy is often added to increase the effectiveness of radiation. Adding chemotherapy is a complex decision that depends on many factors including:

- The tumor size and extent of local tumor spread - Lymph node involvement, the size of the lymph nodes, and whether tumor has spilled out of the lymph node into the surrounding tissues - The overall health of the patient and the patient’s ability to handle the side effects of chemotherapy
02-01-08.heading: Chemotherapy

chunks:
Chemotherapy
Your cancer treatment team will discuss your case together and determine whether you would beneﬁt from treatment with chemotherapy. Chemotherapy is usually delivered weekly, or every three weeks, during radiation. It is important to know that chemotherapy alone does not cure head and neck cancer.
02-01-09.heading: Chemotherapy

chunks:
Medication Followed by Surgery or Radiation
In some uncommon situations, systemic therapy is given before surgery or radiation. Systemic therapies include immunotherapy, chemotherapy, and targeted biologic therapy. This is called a “neoadjuvant” approach to treatment.
Systemic therapy is also given after surgery or radiation. This is called “adjuvant” treatment.
02-01-10.heading: Medication Followed by Surgery or Radiation

chunks:
Medication Followed by Surgery or Radiation
Generally speaking, the goal of this approach is to shrink the tumor before surgery or radiation. Shrinking the tumor may make it easier to completely remove or treat.
02-01-11.heading: Medication Followed by Surgery or Radiation

chunks:
Medication Followed by Surgery or Radiation
Most commonly, these medications are given intravenously, or into the blood through needles in the veins, every 1-3 weeks. The length of treatment with medications before surgery or radiation is commonly 6-12 weeks, but in some scenarios, may last many months.
02-01-12.heading: Medication Followed by Surgery or Radiation

02-02-03.heading: Introduction to palliative cancer

chunks:
Palliative Cancer Treatment: Why?
Sometimes head and neck cancer spreads too far or a patient’s health prevents doctors from offering aggressive cancer treatment. When head and neck cancer cannot be cured with surgery or radiation, doctors may recommend palliative cancer treatment.
02-02-04.heading: Palliative Cancer Treatment: Why?

chunks:
Palliative Cancer Treatment: Why?
With palliative cancer treatment, doctors focus on controlling symptoms and improving quality of life. It is important to know that while we don’t expect palliative treatment to be curative, in some circumstances, it may prolong survival or provide long-term disease control.
02-02-05.heading: Palliative Cancer Treatment: Why?

chunks:
Palliative Cancer Treatment: What is It?
There are several different types of palliative cancer treatment: - Medication, or palliative systemic therapy - Palliative radiation therapy - Palliative surgery - Best supportive care - Hospice
02-02-06.heading: Palliative Cancer Treatment: What is It?

chunks:
Palliative Systemic Therapy
Palliative systemic therapy is the most common type of palliative cancer treatment. It involves chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy.

It is used when cancers are very advanced in the head and neck, when the cancer has spread to other organs, or when surgery or radiation are unlikely to be curative. The choice of drugs and intensity depends on the patient’s symptoms, tumor, and overall health.
02-02-08.heading: Palliative Systemic Therapy

chunks:
Palliative Systemic Therapy
Treatment with palliative systemic therapy traditionally means the cancer is incurable. However, newer treatments such as immunotherapy can sometimes make the cancer disappear completely, for years or more.
02-02-09.heading: Palliative Systemic Therapy

chunks:
Palliative Radiation Therapy
Palliative radiation aims to temporarily shrink the cancer. It also aims to reduce symptoms from the cancer, such as pain. There are a number of different ways palliative radiation can be delivered.
It is often a short course of treatment; most commonly completed in 1-2 weeks of daily treatment.
02-02-10.heading: Palliative Radiation Therapy

chunks:
Palliative Surgery
Palliative surgery is a less common treatment option for head and neck cancers. It shares the same goals of other palliative treatment options: to reduce symptoms from the cancer and improve quality of life.
02-02-11.heading: Palliative Surgery

chunks:
Best Supportive Care
Best supportive care aims to prevent and address the symptoms and side effects of head and neck cancer and improve quality of life. Unlike palliative systemic therapy, radiation, and surgery, best supportive care does not directly treat the cancer.
Supportive care can include pain management, mental health support, nutrition, respiratory support with oxygen, swallow and speech support. The palliative care team can help with symptoms.
02-02-13.heading: Best Supportive Care

chunks:
Hospice
Hospice care also aims to treat the symptoms and side effects of head and neck cancer and improve quality of life. Usually, your doctors will only recommend hospice when you are expected to live for a short period. Hospice care can be given at home or in a facility.
02-02-14.heading: Hospice

chunks:
Surgical oncologist
A surgical oncologist is a surgeon who diagnoses and surgically treats your cancer. Surgical oncologists:

• Take biopsies to help diagnose cancer
• Discuss potential surgical treatments
• Explain the beneﬁts and risks of potential surgical treatment
• Explain to you how to prepare for surgery
• Discuss with you what to expect after surgery
• Oversee your recovery from surgery
03-01-02.heading: Surgical oncologist

chunks:
Medical oncologist
An oncologist is a cancer doctor that specializes in diagnosing and treating cancer with medications like chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, or hormone therapy. Medical oncologists:

• Plan and discuss with you treatment options
• Help you understand the risks and beneﬁts of each treatment option
• Oversee your cancer treatment
• Help manage any side effects from and after your treatment
03-01-03.heading: Medical oncologist

chunks:
Radiation oncologist
Radiation oncologists are doctors that treat cancer with radiation therapy. Radiation oncologists:

• Help decide if you would beneﬁt from radiation therapy and if so which kind
• Explain to you your radiation therapy options and how it works
• Design and discuss with you your treatment plan
• Oversee treatment and help you to manage radiation therapy side effects
03-01-04.heading: Radiation oncologist

chunks:
Speech and language pathologist (SLP)
Speech and language pathologists help with cancer and treatment effects on your voice, swallowing, and communication skills. Speech and language pathologists will meet with you before, during, and after treatment to:

• Evaluate and treat swallowing difﬁculties
• Support communication after surgeries or treatment affecting the mouth and throat
• Teach you safe eating and drinking strategies
• Create a personalized plan to meet your communication and swallowing goals
03-01-05.heading: Speech and language pathologist (SLP)

chunks:
Dentist
Dentists are doctors who specialize in treatment of the teeth, gums, and mouth. Dentists:

• Detect early signs of potential oral cancer
• Manage any oral complications that come up during and after cancer treatment
• If necessary, can help correct any anatomical changes or changes in eating and speaking with prosthetic dentistry
03-01-06.heading: Dentist

chunks:
Oral maxillofacial surgeon
Oral and maxillofacial surgeons are specialists in treating conditions that affect the mouth, jaw, and face. They work with your medical and dental teams to protect your ability to speak, chew, and maintain oral health. Oral and maxillofacial surgeons:

• Treat complications affecting the mouth, teeth, or jaw
• Place dental implants or preparing for dentures after surgery
• Support cosmetic and functional recovery to improve quality of life.
03-01-07.heading: Oral maxillofacial surgeon

chunks:
Dietician
A dietician is a healthcare professional that specializes in food and nutrition. Ask your provider to place a referral if you would like to be contacted. Dieticians help:

• Improve and maintain your nutritional status before, during, and after your cancer treatment
• Manage changes in your weight or appetite
• Help you develop an eating plan that meets your needs
• Answer your questions on diet and nutrition throughout your treatment and recovery
03-01-08.heading: Dietician

chunks:
Social worker
A social worker helps you and your family cope with and manage practical and emotional challenges that come with cancer and its treatment. Social workers:

• Connect you with support groups and community services
• Help you navigate and ﬁnd resources for transportation, housing and ﬁnancial assistance
• Assist with paperwork and insurance concerns
• Advocate for you and your family's’ needs
03-01-09.heading: Social worker

chunks:
Counselor or Therapist
A counselor or therapist supports your emotional and mental wellbeing and help you address emotional, psychological, and social challenges. This may be your psycho-oncologist. Counselors or therapists:

• Provide a safe space to talk
• Help you manage stress, anxiety, and depression
• Support you mentally and emotionally through your treatment and beyond.
03-01-10.heading: Counselor or Therapist

chunks:
Chaplain
A chaplain supports you and your loved ones’ spiritual and emotional well being--regardless of religious background or beliefs. Chaplains help:

• Provide emotional support during difﬁcult moments
• Explore questions about meaning, purpose, or hope
• Support your spiritual or religious practices through treatment and treatment decisions
• Connect you with religious or spiritual resources in your community
03-01-11.heading: Chaplain

chunks:
Occupational therapist
An occupational therapist helps you stay as independent, active, and safe as possible throughout your treatment. Occupational therapists:

• Offer strategies to manage physical changes (such as weakness, limited movement and fatigue)
• Help to adapt your home environment for comfort and safety
• Recommend tools or equipment to make everyday tasks easier and safer
• Support your return to work, school, or hobbies
03-01-12.heading: Occupational therapist

chunks:
Physical therapist
A physical therapist helps you regain strength, balance, and mobility during and after cancer treatment. Physical therapists:

• Reduce pain or stiffness during and after treatment
• Help with walking or movement challenges
• Teach exercises to improve strength, mobility, and coordination
• Teach safe ways to stay active and return to daily routines
03-01-13.heading: Physical therapist

chunks:
Physical medicine and rehabilitation specialist
Physical medicine and rehabilitation specialists are doctors that manage your medical issues throughout the treatment and the rehabilitation process. They work with physical therapists, occupational therapists, and other specialists to optimize recovery.

Physical medicine and rehabilitation specialists:
• Develop a rehabilitation plan to improve movement and function
• Manage and limit pain or discomfort from cancer treatment or surgery
• Recommend equipment to help mobility challenges
03-01-14.heading: Physical medicine and rehabilitation specialist

• Closes off your lungs when you swallow

04-01-05.heading: Treatment options

chunks:
What are my surgical options?
Transoral Laser Total Laryngectomy Partial Laryngectomy Microsurgery (TLM)
04-01-06.heading: What are my surgical options?

chunks:
What is the difference between a partial and total laryngectomy?
A partial laryngectomy is surgery to remove part of your voice box (larynx). This may be done to remove cancer while trying to save your ability to speak and swallow.
A total laryngectomy means the entire voice box (vocal cords) is removed. This is done when cancer involves most or all of the larynx.
04-01-07.heading: What is the difference between a partial and total laryngectomy?

chunks:
What changes after a total laryngectomy?
In a partial laryngectomy, a temporary stoma may be used to help with breathing while you heal.
In a total laryngectomy, a permanent stoma is created because the entire voice box is removed, and this becomes your only way to breathe. Moreover, a prosthesis is needed to speak.
04-01-08.heading: What changes after a total laryngectomy?

chunks:
What is transoral laser microsurgery?
• It is a minimally invasive surgery used to remove tumors from the throat or voice box through the mouth (no open cuts on the neck).
• A microscope is used for precise vision
• A laser is used to cut and remove the tumor
• Usually done under general anesthesia
04-01-09.heading: What is transoral laser microsurgery?

chunks:
When is TLM used?
TLM is used most often to treat:
• Early-stage laryngeal cancer (especially on the vocal cords – glottic cancer)
• Supraglottic cancer (above the vocal cords)
• Benign vocal cord growths (like polyps or papillomas)
• Sometimes used for oropharyngeal cancers (like base of tongue or tonsils)
04-01-10.heading: When is TLM used?

chunks:
Speaking After Surgery
There are a few permanent changes after a total laryngectomy surgery.
• You will learn to speak a new way.
• By 3 weeks post-surgery, you may begin using your artiﬁcial prosthesis placed at the time of surgery.
• This allows you a more natural type of speech.
04-01-12.heading: Speaking After Surgery

chunks:
Prosthesis Considerations and Management
Occasionally, patients prefer not to have a prosthesis placed or the surgeon does not consider it safe to place the prosthesis at the time of our initial surgery.

This can always be done at a later date with some risk. If you have this prosthesis, be sure the passage remains open by keeping a catheter or special tube in the opening at all times should the prosthesis become displaced.
04-01-13.heading: Prosthesis Considerations and Management

chunks:
Post-Laryngectomy Hospital Stay
You will be in the hospital approximately 7-10 days. A soft plastic tube called a Lary tube will be placed in your stoma. This device helps to keep the surgical site open and permits the use of a HME (heat and moisture exchanger) ﬁlter.
04-01-15.heading: Post-Laryngectomy Hospital Stay

chunks:
Stoma Care
It is very important that you learn to care for your stoma as part of your daily hygiene. When released from the hospital you should begin caring for yourself. Your social worker will arrange for the supplies you will need to be delivered to your home Make sure to:

• Replace HME if it becomes clogged with mucus.
• Sleep with your head elevated to prevent swelling.
• Wash your hands each time you touch your stoma
04-01-16.heading: Stoma Care

chunks:
Daily Stoma Care
The following should be performed at least twice a day:
• Remove soft plastic tube for cleaning so you can see only the stoma
• Look in the mirror and spray salt water (see recipe later) into your stoma
• Cough into a tissue held over your stoma
• Clean your stoma with q-tips, 4x4's and/or a washcloth
• Use a mixture of 1/2 hydrogen peroxide and 1/2 water to cleanse stitches and/or staples twice a day until they are removed.
• Place a thin coat of Vaseline or Aquaphor around the stoma and neck to protect and moisturize.
04-01-17.heading: Daily Stoma Care

chunks:
Tips to Maintain Humidity
• Leave your HME ﬁlter in place at all times except when you are cleaning your stoma or if you need to cough.
• Get in the shower and breathe water droplets. Some people are more comfortable wearing a baby bib with the plastic side facing out or a shower collar that can be special ordered.

• Use a bedside humidiﬁer.
• These are very important steps in preventing mucous from plugging your only breathing passage.

Extra moisture is very important. Spray salt water directly into the stoma at least 4 times a day::
• (1/4 tsp salt in 1 cup tap water, changed daily)

Eating and Drinking After Surgery
In order for the surgery site to heal you will not be able to eat or drink by mouth until you are evaluated by your doctor or speech therapist. When it is safe for you to eat by mouth, you may notice a little tightness when you swallow. Don't panic!

• After surgery, you may experience difﬁculty swallowing due to scarring, swelling, or the effects of radiation.
• To make eating easier, try grinding meats, using gravy or sauces to moisten foods, and experimenting with different textures.
• It’s also common for taste to change after surgery. Using more spices and ﬂavorings can help make food more enjoyable.

• Be aware that certain foods, like acidic items or carbonated drinks, may cause bloating or belching. If this happens, over-the-counter remedies like Tums may provide relief.
• If swallowing becomes especially difﬁcult, contact your nurse or speech therapist to discuss treatment options.
04-01-24.heading: Post-Surgery Comfort

Smelling and Breathing Post Surgery
Your sense of smell is usually affected after this surgery.
• Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors are recommended. Your only breathing passage is through your neck.

• Most laryngectomy patients feel more comfortable wearing an emergency bracelet or having information in their wallet to speak for them in case of emergency.
• This will also inform emergency personnel that artiﬁcial oxygen would have to be delivered through the neck.

After a laryngectomy your body is attempting to adapt to your new way of breathing, this may cause a runny nose. You can use over the counter Claritin to help with the drainage.

• The mouth, or oral cavity, is made up of the lips, cheeks, palate, teeth, and tongue.
• Oral cavity cancer affects the lips, front 2/3rds of the tongue, the gums, the lining inside the cheeks/lips, the ﬂoor of the mouth, the bony top of the mouth, and the bony ridges that hold the teeth.

What is a glossectomy?
• Surgical removal of part or all of the tongue.

○ Partial: resection of a portion of the tongue ○ Hemi: removal of one side of the tongue ○ Total: complete tongue removed
• Surgeons aim to preserve as much of the tongue as possible during the procedure.

• The maxilla is the upper jawbone. A maxillectomy refers to the removal of part or all of the maxilla.

• After surgery, some patients might need an obturator (prosthetic device) to aid in restoring speech and chewing.

• This is a more extensive surgery involving tumor removal throughout multiple connected structures in the mouth (tongue, ﬂoor of mouth, jawbone, or soft tissue).

• A neck dissection is a surgical procedure done to remove lymph nodes and surrounding tissue in the neck that may be at risk of containing cancer.
• It is done to prevent cancer from spreading.
• It is done under general anesthesia.
• The surgeon makes an incision along the neck to access and remove lymph nodes.

• Pain and mild swelling at the incision site. ○ Swelling peaks ~4 days post surgery.
• Numbness in the surgery area.
• The skin around the surgery site will be tight and ﬁrm to the touch.

○ This will soften over 4-6 months.

General instructions for recovery
• Use additional pillows if needed to keep your head raised when you lie down for the ﬁrst few weeks after surgery.
• This helps prevent increased swelling.

Medications to take post-surgery
• Take over-the-counter and prescription medications as instructed

• While on pain meds, avoid driving.

○ Drink enough ﬂuids ○ Take over-the-counter stool softeners ○ Eat foods high in ﬁber ○ Limit foods high in fat and processed sugars

Incision care
• You may shower 48 hours post-surgery. Any soaps can be used. Do not scrub the incision site, just let the water run down your neck.

• You may have a drain in place which would be removed ~4-5 days after your surgery.
○ The color of the drainage may change from red, a rose color, or yellow, which is a normal progression.

Incision care (cont.)
• You may use a gauze sponge or other dressing to prevent leaking.

○ More redness, swelling, pain ○ Fluid or blood ○ Warmth ○ Pus or a foul smell

04-03-12.heading: Incision care (cont.)

chunks:
Eating and drinking post-surgery
• Please follow a regular diet while your drain is in place.

• You might be more easily fatigued after surgery. This is normal. Please rest as needed but also be sure you’re up and moving to improve blood ﬂow and breathing.

What is the oropharynx?
• The oropharynx is the middle part of your throat.
• It includes: ○ The back of your tongue ○ Your tonsils ○ The roof of your mouth (soft palate) ○ The walls of your throat
• This area helps you talk, breathe, eat, and swallow.
04-04-02.heading: What is the oropharynx?

chunks:
What is Transoral Robotic Surgery?
• TORS stands for Transoral Robotic Surgery.
• It helps surgeons remove cancer through the mouth.
• It is a good option when the cancer is in a hard-to-reach area.
• TORS avoids large cuts and can help you heal faster.
04-04-03.heading: What is Transoral Robotic Surgery?

chunks:
Where is TORS used?
• Best areas: ○ Tonsils ○ Base of the tongue ○ Roof of the mouth (palate) ○ Back of the throat (pharyngeal wall) ○ Voice box (supraglottis)
• Some deep areas may still need laser surgery (TLM)
04-04-04.heading: Where is TORS used?

chunks:
Weighing the Risks and Beneﬁts
BENEFITS RISKS
• No large cuts to the face or jaw
• May reduce or avoid the need for chemo or radiation
• Often no need for a breathing tube (tracheostomy)
• Faster return to talking and eating
• Less pain and bleeding
• Shorter hospital stay and recovery

• Bleeding: especially around 10 days after surgery
• Taste changes (dysgeusia)
• Trouble swallowing (may need a feeding tube at ﬁrst)
• Nasal food reﬂux or speech changes (rare)
• Leak or ﬁstula (more likely if neck surgery is done too)
04-04-05.heading: Weighing the Risks and Beneﬁts

Who is a good candidate for TORS?
• Not everyone is a good ﬁt
• We look at: ○ Tumor location and size ○ How wide the mouth opens (trismus) ○ Shape of the jaw and tongue ○ Head movement (can you tilt your head back?) ○ Imaging to check blood vessels and tumor location
**Disclaimer: The risks and benefits listed are general and may not apply to everyone. Your healthcare team will evaluate your individual condition to decide if TORS is right for you.
04-04-06.heading: Who is a good candidate for TORS?

• Tumor too close to the spine or big blood vessels
• Tumor involves too much of the tongue or throat wall
• Tumor is ﬁxed (stuck) to nearby tissues
• Carotid artery too close to tumor
• Not safe for general anesthesia
• Can’t open mouth enough to reach tumor
**Disclaimer: The risks and benefits listed are general and may not apply to everyone. Your healthcare team will evaluate your individual condition to decide if TORS is right for you.

chunks:
What are salivary glands?
Salivary glands make saliva, which helps you chew, swallow, and digest food. You have 3 main pairs:
• Parotid glands (in front of your ears)
• Submandibular glands (under your jaw)
• Sublingual glands (under your tongue)
These glands can sometimes develop tumors, which may be benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous).
04-05-04.heading: What are salivary glands?

chunks:
What is a parotidectomy?
Superﬁcial Parotidectomy Total Parotidectomy A parotidectomy is surgery to remove the parotid gland, the largest salivary gland. There are two types:
• Superﬁcial parotidectomy
• Total parotidectomy
04-05-06.heading: What is a parotidectomy?

chunks:
Superﬁcial vs. Total Parotidectomy
TOTAL SUPERFICIAL
• The entire parotid gland is removed.
• This may be needed if:

• Only the outer (superﬁcial) part of the gland is removed.
• Used when the tumor is small and not deep.
• The surgeon carefully avoids the facial nerve, which runs through the gland and controls smiling, blinking, and other facial movements.

○ The tumor is deep inside the gland ○ The cancer is more aggressive
• The facial nerve is still preserved when possible, but sometimes needs to be partially removed if involved by the tumor.
04-05-07.heading: Superﬁcial vs. Total Parotidectomy

• You may feel numbness or weakness in your face—this is usually temporary, but can sometimes last longer.
• A drain may be placed for 1–2 days to remove extra ﬂuid.
• You may have a scar near your ear or jaw, which usually heals well over time.
• Most patients go home within a day or two.
04-05-08.heading: What to expect after a parotidectomy?

04-06-03.heading: Basic Concepts, Deﬁnitions,

chunks:
What is a ﬂap?
A ﬂap is a piece of tissue used to ﬁx a wound or cover a missing area after surgery. A ﬂap is different from a graft because it has its own blood supply (a graft does not). Blood ﬂows into the ﬂap through an artery and out of the ﬂap through a vein to keep it alive.
04-06-04.heading: What is a ﬂap?

chunks:
What can a ﬂap be made of?
Soft tissue (skin, muscle, fat) Bone Both soft tissue and bone
04-06-05.heading: What can a ﬂap be made of?

chunks:
What is a graft?
A graft is a piece of tissue used to repair or rebuild an area, but it does not have its own blood supply. A skin graft is very thin (like a piece of paper) and does not need blood vessels. It can use oxygen and nutrients from the tissue it is placed on.
Because it is so thin, a skin graft is mostly used for surface repairs, not deep wounds.
04-06-06.heading: What is a graft?

chunks:
Bone or Cartilage Grafts
Sometimes bone or cartilage can be used as a graft. Bone or cartilage grafts are small pieces without blood supply. They get oxygen and nutrients from the soft tissue around them.
04-06-07.heading: Bone or Cartilage Grafts

chunks:
Free Flap
A free ﬂap is taken from a distant body part (like the forearm or lower leg). Blood vessels are cut to move the ﬂap to the needed area. The ﬂap vessels are connected to blood vessels in the neck (artery to artery, vein to vein).
This process is like a transplant, but since it comes from the patient’s own body, there is no risk of rejection and no anti-rejection medications are needed.
04-06-08.heading: Free Flap

chunks:
Pedicled Flap
A pedicled ﬂap is taken from a nearby area (like the chest or shoulder). The pedicled ﬂap stays attached to its original blood vessels.
04-06-09.heading: Pedicled Flap

chunks:
Key Differences Between Free Flaps and Pedicled Flaps
A free ﬂap gives more freedom to shape and position the tissue. When bone is needed a free ﬂap is usually necessary (unless the piece of bone is very small).
04-06-10.heading: Key Differences Between Free Flaps and Pedicled Flaps

chunks:
Situations When the Free Flap is a Better Option than the Pedicled Flap or Graft
A skin graft may be too thin and not work well for deep wounds. Skin grafts in the mouth can cause scarring and limit tongue movement. Skin grafts cannot be placed directly on bone because bone does not provide enough blood supply.
04-06-11.heading: Situations When the Free Flap is a Better Option than the Pedicled Flap or Graft

chunks:
Situations When the Free Flap is a Better Option than the Pedicled Flap or Graft
Grafts may not heal well if the area has had or will have radiation therapy. A pedicled ﬂap may be too thick or not reach the area needing repair.
04-06-12.heading: Situations When the Free Flap is a Better Option than the Pedicled Flap or Graft

04-06-13.heading: Flap Surgery Involving the

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Flap Surgery Involving the Inside of the Mouth or Throat
How does surgery affect eating, drinking, and breathing? The mouth and throat are important for eating, drinking, speaking, and breathing.

Surgery in these areas can cause swelling, which may make it hard to breathe, sometimes requiring a temporary tracheostomy tube (a breathing tube in the neck). It can also affect the ability to swallow food and liquids, making a feeding tube necessary during healing.
04-06-14.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Flap Surgery Involving the Inside of the Mouth or Throat

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer When can I eat by mouth?
The flap (usually skin) is stitched into place to repair the surgical wound in the mouth. Stitches dissolve in about a month, but healing takes 2 to 3 weeks or longer. The wound must be fully sealed to prevent saliva from leaking into the wound. Your surgeon will decide when it is safe for you to start eating and drinking again.
04-06-15.heading: I Can Manage Cancer When can I eat by mouth?

chunks:
Can I swallow my own saliva while I am healing, or should I spit it out?
Yes, you can swallow your saliva. It is not recommended to constantly spit or suction it out, unless you cannot swallow. This could cause dehydration over time.
04-06-16.heading: Can I swallow my own saliva while I am healing, or should I spit it out?

chunks:
Lower Jaw (Mandible)
Reconstruction
04-07-02.heading: Lower Jaw (Mandible)

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Lower Jaw (Mandible) Reconstruction
Why is a free flap used to repair the lower jaw? Reconstructing the lower jaw usually requires a free flap because these cancers need radiation therapy after surgery to prevent the cancer from returning.
Radiation would destroy a bone graft because the graft does not have a blood supply, but the free flap does have blood supply.
04-07-03.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Lower Jaw (Mandible) Reconstruction

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Lower Jaw (Mandible) Reconstruction
Also, a free flap is used when there is a gap in the bone bigger than about 5 cm (2 inches) because larger grafts may not survive.
The bone-containing flaps that are commonly used for jaw reconstruction are the fibula, scapula, and a small amount from the radius/forearm flaps (AKA osteocutaneous radial forearm free flap).
04-07-04.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Lower Jaw (Mandible) Reconstruction Continued

chunks:
Which type of ﬂap will be used for the mandible? The ﬁbula ﬂap
Surgeons usually use the ﬁbula ﬂap to rebuild the jaw. The ﬁbula is a strong bone in the lower leg that can be shaped to ﬁt the jaw. We also take some soft tissue (skin, fat, and fascia) from the leg to help with the reconstruction.
04-07-05.heading: Which type of ﬂap will be used for the mandible? The ﬁbula ﬂap

chunks:
The Fibula Flap
The ﬁbula’s blood vessels are long, which helps position the new jaw correctly. Another beneﬁt is that while one surgeon removes the tumor, another can prepare the ﬁbula ﬂap at the same time. This can save 1 to 2 hours in surgery.
04-07-06.heading: The Fibula Flap Continued

chunks:
The Scapula Flap
Another option is the scapula ﬂap (from the shoulder blade). However, since it's on the back, it takes more time in surgery because surgeons can’t work on it at the same time as tumor removal.

The scapula ﬂap is often used if the lower leg isn’t healthy enough for a ﬁbula ﬂap. This is because leg arteries can have more blockage (atherosclerosis), while the scapula’s artery is usually healthier.
04-07-07.heading: The Scapula Flap

chunks:
The Scapula Flap
Unlike the ﬁbula ﬂap, the scapula ﬂap doesn’t need a special scan (CT angiogram) to check blood ﬂow because the artery for the scapula ﬂap is not vital to any other body part.
The scapula ﬂap is also a better choice when a lot of soft tissue is needed, as it provides more skin and muscle than the ﬁbula.
04-07-08.heading: The Scapula Flap Continued

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Other Options for Jaw Reconstruction- the Radial Forearm Flap
Another option is the radial forearm flap (from the inner forearm). This flap includes a thin piece of bone, so it’s not usually the first choice for the jaw. Instead, it’s often used for reconstructing the upper jaw, cheekbones, or eye sockets.
04-07-09.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Other Options for Jaw Reconstruction- the Radial Forearm Flap

chunks:
How is the ﬂap bone connected to the jaw?
A titanium plate is used to connect the pieces of bone together. This plate spans the gap across the mandible where the tumor was removed. The plate is screwed into the remaining parts of the mandible as well as the bone of the ﬂap after it is shaped to ﬁt the defect.
04-07-10.heading: How is the ﬂap bone connected to the jaw?

chunks:
The Titanium Plate
The size and position of a mandible resection depends on the location of the tumor, but this is an example of a large reconstruction plate.

Every resection is a little different. In this case, the entire chin is being removed. The bone that needs to be removed is determined by the cancer surgeon, based on the location and size of the tumor. Click here to return to forearm ﬂap slide 81
04-07-11.heading: The Titanium Plate Continued

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Is the titanium plate safe?
Yes, the titanium plate is safe and stays in the body permanently for most patients. It does not cause allergies or reactions and cannot be rejected by the body.
04-07-12.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Is the titanium plate safe?

chunks:
Is the titanium plate safe?
The titanium plate is not magnetic, so it won’t set off metal detectors and is safe for MRIs.

Occasionally, the plate can become infected over time (rarely) and need to be removed. Another rare complication is when the plate becomes loose over time, requiring removal, or the plate breaks. These situations are rare.
04-07-13.heading: Is the titanium plate safe? Continued

chunks:
Soft Tissue Repair in the Tongue, Cheek, or Under the Tongue
If there is a soft tissue defect in the tongue, cheek, or under the tongue (ﬂoor of the mouth) some skin or muscle from the ﬂap is sutured in place to patch the soft tissue defect. The sutures will all dissolve on their own.
04-07-14.heading: Soft Tissue Repair in the Tongue, Cheek, or Under the Tongue

chunks:
Will I look like myself after mandible reconstruction surgery or will I be disﬁgured?
For most patients, the changes to appearance after mandible reconstruction are minimal. Signiﬁcant changes are rare and usually only happen if the tumor or wound affects the external skin or soft tissue of the face or neck. This is typically seen in very large tumors.
04-07-15.heading: Will I look like myself after mandible reconstruction surgery or will I be disﬁgured?

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Will I have visible scars?
Generally, this surgery is done through the inside of the mouth and an incision on the neck. It is not usually necessary to place any scars on the face unless the tumor is invading the skin of the face or neck (this is not common).
04-07-16.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Will I have visible scars?

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Will I have visible scars?
A neck incision is necessary to find blood vessels in the neck to re-establish blood flow to the flap. These neck incisions heal very well and leave a faint scar that is generally not obvious after it heals.
Usually, lymph nodes need to be removed from the neck as part of the cancer surgery. The same neck incision is used for this as well.
04-07-17.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Will I have visible scars?

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Will my face shape change?
The shape of the reconstructed mandible is based on the shape of each individual patient’s jaw. The titanium plate is custom made to each patient’s anatomy.

This type of facial surgery is generally less painful than most patients expect. There is certainly some pain, but it is usually well controlled with pain medicine.

The Fibula Flap. How is the ﬁbula used for reconstruction?
The ﬁbula is the smaller of the two lower leg bones (the larger bone is the tibia). It can be safely removed and used for reconstruction. The central part of the ﬁbula is removed, saving the bottom 3-4 inches by the ankle, and a similar length by the knee.
04-08-11.heading: The Fibula Flap. How is the ﬁbula used for reconstruction?

chunks:
Will this affect blood ﬂow to my leg?
The lower leg has 3 arteries that carry blood down to the foot. The artery called the peroneal artery supplies the ﬁbula ﬂap. Because the leg has 3 main arteries, and if the other two arteries are healthy, blood ﬂow to the foot remains normal after surgery.
04-08-12.heading: Will this affect blood ﬂow to my leg?

chunks:
How do we make sure it’s safe?
We will check your pulses on your foot and order a scan called a CT Angiogram, which examines the arteries in the legs. We do this to make sure that it is safe to take the peroneal vessels supplying the ﬁbula ﬂap without hurting the circulation to the foot.
04-08-13.heading: How do we make sure it’s safe?

chunks:
What will my leg look like after surgery?
If no skin is needed for reconstruction, you will have a in scar, in a straight line, running down the outside of the calf, from below the knee to above the ankle. The example on the right shows a scar after two weeks of healing—this is not the ﬁnal result.
04-08-14.heading: What will my leg look like after surgery?

chunks:
What happens if skin is needed for reconstruction?
If skin is necessary for reconstruction, the resulting skin wound usually cannot be closed. This leaves a shallow, open wound, with exposed muscle, after the ﬂap is taken.

To repair this, we may take a skin graft from the thigh. This skin graft is paper thin and is used to patch the leg wound. It will always look somewhat like a patch, but the color will even out over time, and the scars will fade and become smooth.
04-08-15.heading: What happens if skin is needed for reconstruction?

chunks:
What are my other options for a skin graft?
More commonly, we are now using a skin substitute called biodegradable tissue matrix (BTM), rather than a skin graft for ﬁbula donor sites. This is an artiﬁcial skin substitute that helps the wound heal.
There is a thin plastic layer covering the BTM. The surgeon will take this off in the clinic. If you notice it falling off, do not be alarmed.
04-08-16.heading: What are my other options for a skin graft?

chunks:
How does BTM work?
The BTM forms a layer of healing tissue called granulation tissue over the wound bed. Once this (granulation tissue) has formed, the body forms skin over the BTM naturally.
04-08-17.heading: How does BTM work?

This process can take several months, depending on the size of the defect. This is an example of what it may look like when it's healed.

The ﬁbula bone functions to provide stability to the ankle, in addition to the many ligaments of the ankle and foot that bind the different bones together. When the ﬁbula is removed, extra stress is placed on these ligaments.
Over time, the ligaments strengthen and compensate for the loss of the ﬁbula. Until this happens, there will be some discomfort and instability.
04-09-08.heading: Will the surgery affect my walking?

chunks:

Patients who have problems with strength or mobility pre-operatively may require weeks or months of using a walker or cane, along with physical therapy. This is not usually expected, but it is a possibility to prepare for.

04-09-09.heading: Will I have have mobility issues?

It is rare to have permanent major functional problems from a scapula ﬂap. There will certainly be some soreness and stiffness, which may last several months. If necessary, we will arrange for physical therapy.
04-09-16.heading: Will my shoulder function be affected?

How sore or stiff will I feel after?
The degree of soreness and stiffness depends on the amount of tissue that is needed for the reconstruction. Smaller tumors and smaller ﬂaps lead to less issues with recovery. Larger surgeries can have more lasting stiffness and soreness.
04-09-17.heading: How sore or stiff will I feel after?

Two rubber drainage tubes are left in the ﬂank at the time of surgery to drain ﬂuid that accumulates in the surgical wound. Usually, one drain is removed after about one week and the second usually stays with the patient after they are discharged home. drain tube

The drain needs to be emptied twice daily (or more depending on the amount of drainage) and the output needs to be recorded. The surgeon will want to know the daily output of the drain in milliliters (ML) for each 24-hour period.

chunks:
Complications
If part of the incision opens, saliva can track into the incision and down into the neck. This is called a ﬁstula and can cause infection. If saliva is draining into blood vessels, it can cause them to clot or rupture, which can damage or kill a ﬂap.

Usually, a ﬁstula does not occur until about 7-10 days after surgery.
• If it does happen, we may simply watch it closely (if it is small) or it may require additional procedures to clean the wound, patch the leak or place new drains.
04-13-09.heading: Complications

chunks:
Flap Clotting
A clot can form in the blood vessel feeding the ﬂap and kill the ﬂap. While this is not the type of clot that can go to your lungs or brain and be life threatening, it can necessitate more surgery. Luckily, this is rare and occurs in about 1 patient out of every 100 cases.
04-13-10.heading: Flap Clotting

chunks:
Flap Clotting
Spontaneous ﬂap clotting is most common the ﬁrst couple days after surgery. After this it is rare unless there is a ﬁstula or infection around the ﬂap vessels, so the risk increases again about a week after surgery, when ﬁstulas and infections tend to develop.
04-13-11.heading: Flap Clotting

chunks:
Flap Clotting Risks
The risks may be higher if you have a condition that leads to blood clotting. ●Make sure your surgeon knows if you have ever had a blood clot in your legs or lungs or if blood clots run in your family. ●Clotting disorders include Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin
mutation, Protein C or S deﬁciency, elevated homocysteine, dysﬁbrinogenemia, and others. These are all rare but very important to know about.
04-13-12.heading: Flap Clotting Risks

chunks:
Flap Checks
Flap checks are done to assess the blood ﬂow to the ﬂap and make sure the ﬂap is alive and healthy. A ﬂap check involves looking at the ﬂap skin to make sure it the appropriate color.
• The skin should look like normal healthy skin.
• If it is very dark or purple or extremely
pale, this can be an indication of a problem.
04-13-13.heading: Flap Checks

chunks:
Flap Checks
A doppler stethoscope is also used to assess blood ﬂow to the ﬂap. This is a non-invasive way to listen to the pulsation of blood through the ﬂap. Sometimes we will need to scratch the ﬂap with a needle to assess the blood ﬂow to the ﬂap.
When this is done you will not feel pain from the needle stick because the ﬂap has no sensation as it has been detached from all nerves.
04-13-14.heading: Flap Checks

After the Hospital and
Follow Up
04-13-15.heading: After the Hospital and

chunks:
Follow-up
You will follow up in your reconstructive surgeon’s ofﬁce 1 week after discharge, then 2-3 weeks after the initial post-op visit, then about 2-3 months later, followed by another 1-3 visits every 6 months. Visits may be more frequent if there are any wound care issues.
Your cancer surgeon and other doctors will have different schedules.
04-13-16.heading: Follow-up

chunks:
Medication Management
It is important to check in with your primary doctor and any specialists, such as cardiologist, pulmonologist, endocrinologist, after discharge from the hospital.
Some of your routine medications may change while you are healing and dosing may be altered during and after the hospital admission.
04-13-17.heading: Medication Management

chunks:
Medication Management
It is very important to re-establish care with your normal medical doctors after discharge.

As surgeons, we are not familiar with management of most of these medications and can provide minimal assistance with questions and concerns regarding management of blood pressure, diabetes, neurological conditions, and other medical problems.

04-14-003.heading: Basic Concepts, Deﬁnitions,

chunks:
What is a ﬂap?
A ﬂap is a piece of tissue used to ﬁx a wound or cover a missing area after surgery. A ﬂap is different from a graft because it has its own blood supply (a graft does not). Blood ﬂows into the ﬂap through an artery and out of the ﬂap through a vein to keep it alive.
04-14-004.heading: What is a ﬂap?

chunks:
What can a ﬂap be made of?
Soft tissue (skin, muscle, fat) Bone Both soft tissue and bone
04-14-005.heading: What can a ﬂap be made of?

chunks:
What is a graft?
A graft is a piece of tissue used to repair or rebuild an area, but it does not have its own blood supply. A skin graft is very thin (like a piece of paper) and does not need blood vessels. It can use oxygen and nutrients from the tissue it is placed on.
Because it is so thin, a skin graft is mostly used for surface repairs, not deep wounds.
04-14-006.heading: What is a graft?

chunks:
Bone or Cartilage Grafts
Sometimes bone or cartilage can be used as a graft. Bone or cartilage grafts are small pieces without blood supply. They get oxygen and nutrients from the soft tissue around them.
04-14-007.heading: Bone or Cartilage Grafts

chunks:
Free Flap
A free ﬂap is taken from a distant body part (like the forearm or lower leg). Blood vessels are cut to move the ﬂap to the needed area. The ﬂap vessels are connected to blood vessels in the neck (artery to artery, vein to vein).
This process is like a transplant, but since it comes from the patient’s own body, there is no risk of rejection and no anti-rejection medications are needed.
04-14-008.heading: Free Flap

chunks:
Pedicled Flap
A pedicled ﬂap is taken from a nearby area (like the chest or shoulder). The pedicled ﬂap stays attached to its original blood vessels.
04-14-009.heading: Pedicled Flap

chunks:
Key Differences Between Free Flaps and Pedicled Flaps
A free ﬂap gives more freedom to shape and position the tissue. When bone is needed a free ﬂap is usually necessary (unless the piece of bone is very small).
04-14-010.heading: Key Differences Between Free Flaps and Pedicled Flaps

chunks:
Situations When the Free Flap is a Better Option than the Pedicled Flap or Graft
A skin graft may be too thin and not work well for deep wounds. Skin grafts in the mouth can cause scarring and limit tongue movement. Skin grafts cannot be placed directly on bone because bone does not provide enough blood supply.
04-14-011.heading: Situations When the Free Flap is a Better Option than the Pedicled Flap or Graft

chunks:
Situations When the Free Flap is a Better Option than the Pedicled Flap or Graft
Grafts may not heal well if the area has had or will have radiation therapy. A pedicled ﬂap may be too thick or not reach the area needing repair.
04-14-012.heading: Situations When the Free Flap is a Better Option than the Pedicled Flap or Graft

Inside of the Mouth
04-14-013.heading: Flap Surgery Involving the

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Flap Surgery Involving the Inside of the Mouth or Throat
How does surgery affect eating, drinking, and breathing? The mouth and throat are important for eating, drinking, speaking, and breathing.

Surgery in these areas can cause swelling, which may make it hard to breathe, sometimes requiring a temporary tracheostomy tube (a breathing tube in the neck). It can also affect the ability to swallow food and liquids, making a feeding tube necessary during healing.
04-14-014.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Flap Surgery Involving the Inside of the Mouth or Throat

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer When can I eat by mouth?
The flap (usually skin) is stitched into place to repair the surgical wound in the mouth. Stitches dissolve in about a month, but healing takes 2 to 3 weeks or longer. The wound must be fully sealed to prevent saliva from leaking into the wound. Your surgeon will decide when it is safe for you to start eating and drinking again.
04-14-015.heading: I Can Manage Cancer When can I eat by mouth?

chunks:
Can I swallow my own saliva while I am healing, or should I spit it out?
Yes, you can swallow your saliva. It is not recommended to constantly spit or suction it out, unless you cannot swallow. This could cause dehydration over time.
04-14-016.heading: Can I swallow my own saliva while I am healing, or should I spit it out?

Lower Jaw (Mandible)
Reconstruction
04-14-018.heading: Lower Jaw (Mandible)

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Lower Jaw (Mandible) Reconstruction
Why is a free flap used to repair the lower jaw? Reconstructing the lower jaw usually requires a free flap because these cancers need radiation therapy after surgery to prevent the cancer from returning.
Radiation would destroy a bone graft because the graft does not have a blood supply, but the free flap does have blood supply.
04-14-019.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Lower Jaw (Mandible) Reconstruction

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Lower Jaw (Mandible) Reconstruction
Also, a free flap is used when there is a gap in the bone bigger than about 5 cm (2 inches) because larger grafts may not survive.
The bone-containing flaps that are commonly used for jaw reconstruction are the fibula, scapula, and a small amount from the radius/forearm flaps (AKA osteocutaneous radial forearm free flap).
04-14-020.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Lower Jaw (Mandible) Reconstruction Continued

chunks:
Which type of ﬂap will be used for the mandible? The ﬁbula ﬂap
Surgeons usually use the ﬁbula ﬂap to rebuild the jaw. The ﬁbula is a strong bone in the lower leg that can be shaped to ﬁt the jaw. We also take some soft tissue (skin, fat, and fascia) from the leg to help with the reconstruction.
04-14-021.heading: Which type of ﬂap will be used for the mandible? The ﬁbula ﬂap

chunks:
The Fibula Flap
The ﬁbula’s blood vessels are long, which helps position the new jaw correctly. Another beneﬁt is that while one surgeon removes the tumor, another can prepare the ﬁbula ﬂap at the same time. This can save 1 to 2 hours in surgery.
04-14-022.heading: The Fibula Flap Continued

chunks:
The Scapula Flap
Another option is the scapula ﬂap (from the shoulder blade). However, since it's on the back, it takes more time in surgery because surgeons can’t work on it at the same time as tumor removal.

The scapula ﬂap is often used if the lower leg isn’t healthy enough for a ﬁbula ﬂap. This is because leg arteries can have more blockage (atherosclerosis), while the scapula’s artery is usually healthier.
04-14-023.heading: The Scapula Flap

chunks:
The Scapula Flap
Unlike the ﬁbula ﬂap, the scapula ﬂap doesn’t need a special scan (CT angiogram) to check blood ﬂow because the artery for the scapula ﬂap is not vital to any other body part.
The scapula ﬂap is also a better choice when a lot of soft tissue is needed, as it provides more skin and muscle than the ﬁbula.
04-14-024.heading: The Scapula Flap Continued

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Other Options for Jaw Reconstruction- the Radial Forearm Flap
Another option is the radial forearm flap (from the inner forearm). This flap includes a thin piece of bone, so it’s not usually the first choice for the jaw. Instead, it’s often used for reconstructing the upper jaw, cheekbones, or eye sockets.
04-14-025.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Other Options for Jaw Reconstruction- the Radial Forearm Flap

chunks:
How is the ﬂap bone connected to the jaw?
A titanium plate is used to connect the pieces of bone together. This plate spans the gap across the mandible where the tumor was removed. The plate is screwed into the remaining parts of the mandible as well as the bone of the ﬂap after it is shaped to ﬁt the defect.
04-14-026.heading: How is the ﬂap bone connected to the jaw?

chunks:
The Titanium Plate
The size and position of a mandible resection depends on the location of the tumor, but this is an example of a large reconstruction plate.

Every resection is a little different. In this case, the entire chin is being removed. The bone that needs to be removed is determined by the cancer surgeon, based on the location and size of the tumor. Click here to return to forearm ﬂap slide 81
04-14-027.heading: The Titanium Plate Continued

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Is the titanium plate safe?
Yes, the titanium plate is safe and stays in the body permanently for most patients. It does not cause allergies or reactions and cannot be rejected by the body.
04-14-028.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Is the titanium plate safe?

chunks:
Is the titanium plate safe?
The titanium plate is not magnetic, so it won’t set off metal detectors and is safe for MRIs.

Occasionally, the plate can become infected over time (rarely) and need to be removed. Another rare complication is when the plate becomes loose over time, requiring removal, or the plate breaks. These situations are rare.
04-14-029.heading: Is the titanium plate safe? Continued

chunks:
Soft Tissue Repair in the Tongue, Cheek, or Under the Tongue
If there is a soft tissue defect in the tongue, cheek, or under the tongue (ﬂoor of the mouth) some skin or muscle from the ﬂap is sutured in place to patch the soft tissue defect. The sutures will all dissolve on their own.
04-14-030.heading: Soft Tissue Repair in the Tongue, Cheek, or Under the Tongue

chunks:
Will I look like myself after mandible reconstruction surgery or will I be disﬁgured?
For most patients, the changes to appearance after mandible reconstruction are minimal. Signiﬁcant changes are rare and usually only happen if the tumor or wound affects the external skin or soft tissue of the face or neck. This is typically seen in very large tumors.
04-14-031.heading: Will I look like myself after mandible reconstruction surgery or will I be disﬁgured?

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Will I have visible scars?
Generally, this surgery is done through the inside of the mouth and an incision on the neck. It is not usually necessary to place any scars on the face unless the tumor is invading the skin of the face or neck (this is not common).
04-14-032.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Will I have visible scars?

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Will I have visible scars?
A neck incision is necessary to find blood vessels in the neck to re-establish blood flow to the flap. These neck incisions heal very well and leave a faint scar that is generally not obvious after it heals.
Usually, lymph nodes need to be removed from the neck as part of the cancer surgery. The same neck incision is used for this as well.
04-14-033.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Will I have visible scars?

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Will my face shape change?
The shape of the reconstructed mandible is based on the shape of each individual patient’s jaw. The titanium plate is custom made to each patient’s anatomy.
It is not possible to make the new jaw the exact same shape as the patient's natural jaw, however, the changes are usually subtle once healing is complete
04-14-034.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Will my face shape change?

chunks:
Swelling of the Face and Neck
Swelling of the face and neck is normal and expected after surgery. Usually, this swelling is the worst 3 days after the surgery and then gradually improves over the next several weeks to months. Swelling may come and go at times- this is normal.
04-14-035.heading: Swelling of the Face and Neck

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer When is swelling the worst?
Sometimes patients find that swelling is worse in the morning when they wake up – because they have been lying down all night. If this is the case, sleep with your head elevated on extra pillows, or even in a reclining chair if necessary. Sometimes patients notice swelling increases throughout the day, and it is better in the morning.
04-14-036.heading: I Can Manage Cancer When is swelling the worst?

chunks:
When should I be worried about swelling?
If swelling is gradually worsening over several consecutive days, this may be a cause for concern, especially if there is also increased pain, redness of the neck or face, or drainage of pus from incisions or drain tubes.
The presence of fevers and/or chills is a warning sign as well. Talk to your surgical team.
04-14-037.heading: When should I be worried about swelling?

chunks:
Is this surgery painful?
This type of facial surgery is generally less painful than most patients expect. There is certainly some pain, but it is usually well controlled with pain medicine.
There may be some pain that comes and goes. Pain may be worse at certain times of day and some days may be worse than others. This is normal.
04-14-038.heading: Is this surgery painful?

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer When is pain concerning?
Pain is worrisome if it is continually increasing over several days. Especially if there is also fevers/chills, swelling that is gradually increasing over several days, or any new drainage from any incisions.
04-14-039.heading: I Can Manage Cancer When is pain concerning?

Reconstruction
04-14-040.heading: Upper Jaw / Midface

chunks:
Upper Jaw/Midface (Maxilla) Reconstruction
Maxillary reconstruction is similar to mandible reconstruction in many ways. The bones are smaller than the mandible, so while titanium plates are still used to join the bone segments together, these are smaller than the plates used for mandible reconstruction.
Plates are still usually custom made for each individual patient.
04-14-041.heading: Upper Jaw/Midface (Maxilla) Reconstruction

chunks:
Upper Jaw/Midface (Maxilla) Reconstruction
Other than these differences, the details of the mandible reconstruction section above apply to patients who are undergoing maxillary reconstruction.
04-14-042.heading: Upper Jaw/Midface (Maxilla) Reconstruction Continued

chunks:
The Fibula Flap. How is the ﬁbula used for reconstruction?
The ﬁbula is the smaller of the two lower leg bones (the larger bone is the tibia). It can be safely removed and used for reconstruction. The central part of the ﬁbula is removed, saving the bottom 3-4 inches by the ankle, and a similar length by the knee.
04-14-044.heading: The Fibula Flap. How is the ﬁbula used for reconstruction?

chunks:
Will this affect blood ﬂow to my leg?
The lower leg has 3 arteries that carry blood down to the foot. The artery called the peroneal artery supplies the ﬁbula ﬂap. Because the leg has 3 main arteries, and if the other two arteries are healthy, blood ﬂow to the foot remains normal after surgery.
04-14-045.heading: Will this affect blood ﬂow to my leg?

chunks:
How do we make sure it’s safe?
We will check your pulses on your foot and order a scan called a CT Angiogram, which examines the arteries in the legs. We do this to make sure that it is safe to take the peroneal vessels supplying the ﬁbula ﬂap without hurting the circulation to the foot.
04-14-046.heading: How do we make sure it’s safe?

chunks:
What will my leg look like after surgery?
If no skin is needed for reconstruction, you will have a in scar, in a straight line, running down the outside of the calf, from below the knee to above the ankle. The example on the right shows a scar after two weeks of healing—this is not the ﬁnal result.
04-14-047.heading: What will my leg look like after surgery?

chunks:
What happens if skin is needed for reconstruction?
If skin is necessary for reconstruction, the resulting skin wound usually cannot be closed. This leaves a shallow, open wound, with exposed muscle, after the ﬂap is taken.

To repair this, we may take a skin graft from the thigh. This skin graft is paper thin and is used to patch the leg wound. It will always look somewhat like a patch, but the color will even out over time, and the scars will fade and become smooth.
04-14-048.heading: What happens if skin is needed for reconstruction?

chunks:
What are my other options for a skin graft?
More commonly, we are now using a skin substitute called biodegradable tissue matrix (BTM), rather than a skin graft for ﬁbula donor sites. This is an artiﬁcial skin substitute that helps the wound heal.
There is a thin plastic layer covering the BTM. The surgeon will take this off in the clinic. If you notice it falling off, do not be alarmed.
04-14-049.heading: What are my other options for a skin graft?

chunks:
How does BTM work?
The BTM forms a layer of healing tissue called granulation tissue over the wound bed. Once this (granulation tissue) has formed, the body forms skin over the BTM naturally.
04-14-050.heading: How does BTM work?

chunks:
How long will this healing process take?
This process can take several months, depending on the size of the defect. This is an example of what it may look like when it's healed.
04-14-051.heading: How long will this healing process take?

chunks:
What to expect after surgery— drain tube
There will be a plastic surgical drain tube placed in the wound at the time of surgery. This is usually removed before you leave the hospital. Drain tube
04-14-052.heading: What to expect after surgery— drain tube

chunks:
What to expect after surgery– wound VAC
There will also be a wound VAC placed on the donor site (the are the skin is taken from) in the hospital. Patients rarely go home with a wound VAC, so you don’t need to learn to manage it. *We have additional information on the wound VAC elsewhere
04-14-053.heading: What to expect after surgery– wound VAC

chunks:
When can I walk?
You can walk and bear weight immediately after surgery, with assistance. Immediately after surgery, patients have many monitors, drains, and IV lines attached to them-- it is easy to trip and fall.
You will need to be helped when getting out of bed while you are in the hospital, especially while in the ICU.
04-14-054.heading: When can I walk?

chunks:
Will I have pain in my leg?
The pain from the ﬁbula ﬂap is usually less severe than people expect. Usually, it is more bothersome after patients start walking more at home, and it can linger for weeks or even months.
04-14-055.heading: Will I have pain in my leg?

chunks:
How long will I have pain in my leg?
This pain resolves with time, but sometimes it can take months or a year. Usually, the pain is mild soreness and lasts about 6 months. It is like having a sprained ankle
04-14-056.heading: How long will I have pain in my leg?

chunks:
Will I need physical therapy?
Physical therapy is sometimes needed, but not always. Generally, healthy, active people regain full mobility more quickly than patients who have a lower baseline level of mobility and activity prior to surgery.
Usually, active, healthy patients can walk without assistance (meaning without a cane or walker) in a few weeks.
04-14-057.heading: Will I need physical therapy?

chunks:
Will the surgery affect my walking?
The ﬁbula bone functions to provide stability to the ankle, in addition to the many ligaments of the ankle and foot that bind the different bones together. When the ﬁbula is removed, extra stress is placed on these ligaments.
Over time, the ligaments strengthen and compensate for the loss of the ﬁbula. Until this happens, there will be some discomfort and instability.
04-14-058.heading: Will the surgery affect my walking?

chunks:
Will I have have mobility issues?
Patients who have problems with strength or mobility pre-operatively may require weeks or months of using a walker or cane, along with physical therapy. This is not usually expected, but it is a possibility to prepare for.
It is very unusual to have any permanent mobility problems after a ﬁbula ﬂap, but healing can be slow.
04-14-059.heading: Will I have have mobility issues?

chunks:
Is leg swelling normal?
Swelling in the ﬁbula ﬂap donor leg is quite common. If you have any swelling in the legs before surgery, it is very likely you will have more severe swelling in the donor leg after surgery. This is usually temporary
04-14-060.heading: Is leg swelling normal?

chunks:
What can I do to help the swelling go down?
You can use an ACE wrap or a compression stocking to help with this.
04-14-061.heading: What can I do to help the swelling go down?

chunks:
How do I use the ACE wrap?
Make sure to wrap the leg starting at the toes, around the foot, and ankle. The goal is to provide more compression to the foot and ankle than to the calf.

Wrapping the leg without wrapping the ankle will lead to worsened swelling because ﬂuid will be trapped below the compression, in the ankle. *We have a leg dressing guide that provides more instructions on how to wrap the leg appropriately
04-14-062.heading: How do I use the ACE wrap?

chunks:
Scapula (Shoulder Blade)
Flap
04-14-063.heading: Scapula (Shoulder Blade)

chunks:
Is the whole scapula used?
When the scapula is needed for reconstruction, it is not removed in its entirety. Only the edge of the bone or the tip of the scapula is taken, leaving most of the scapula intact.
04-14-064.heading: Is the whole scapula used?

chunks:
What will the incision look like?
The incision will run along the ﬂank, from the axilla (under-arm) down about 10 inches or so. The donor site wound can usually be closed completely, without a skin graft.
04-14-065.heading: What will the incision look like?

chunks:
Will my shoulder function be affected?
It is rare to have permanent major functional problems from a scapula ﬂap. There will certainly be some soreness and stiffness, which may last several months. If necessary, we will arrange for physical therapy.
04-14-066.heading: Will my shoulder function be affected?

chunks:
How sore or stiff will I feel after?
The degree of soreness and stiffness depends on the amount of tissue that is needed for the reconstruction. Smaller tumors and smaller ﬂaps lead to less issues with recovery. Larger surgeries can have more lasting stiffness and soreness.
04-14-067.heading: How sore or stiff will I feel after?

chunks:
Will I have drain tubes?
Two rubber drainage tubes are left in the ﬂank at the time of surgery to drain ﬂuid that accumulates in the surgical wound. Usually, one drain is removed after about one week and the second usually stays with the patient after they are discharged home. drain tube
04-14-068.heading: Will I have drain tubes?

chunks:
How do I take care of my drain?
The drain needs to be emptied twice daily (or more depending on the amount of drainage) and the output needs to be recorded. The surgeon will want to know the daily output of the drain in milliliters (ML) for each 24-hour period.
When the drain output is less than 50 ML per 24-hour period, it may be ready to be removed.
04-14-069.heading: How do I take care of my drain?

chunks:
Will ﬂuid accumulate after the drain tube is removed?
Occasionally, ﬂuid continues to accumulate even after the drain is removed. This can lead to swelling of the skin that feels soft, like a water balloon. When you stand up the swelling will drift down to the lowest portion of the surgical site.
04-14-070.heading: Will ﬂuid accumulate after the drain tube is removed?

chunks:
What should I do if ﬂuid accumulates after the drain is removed?
This ﬂuid (called a seroma) usually needs to be drained but the procedure is easy and usually done in the ofﬁce.

The skin overlying the area is usually numb from the surgery and the ﬂuid can be drained through a small needle inserted through the skin. Sometimes this can require several drainage procedures if the ﬂuid keeps reaccumulating.
04-14-071.heading: What should I do if ﬂuid accumulates after the drain is removed?

chunks:
How long can I wait to get the ﬂuid drained?
This is not urgent – you do not need to come in the same day for this problem. Waiting even a week or two will be okay
04-14-072.heading: How long can I wait to get the ﬂuid drained?

chunks:
What wound care do I need to do for the scapula ﬂap?
Aside from drain care, all you need to do is apply petroleum jelly (Vaseline or Aquaphor) to the incision several times a day. This is to keep it from scabbing or drying out.
04-14-073.heading: What wound care do I need to do for the scapula ﬂap?

04-14-074.heading: Reconstruction of Soft Tissue (No Bone is Reconstructed)

chunks:
What is a forearm ﬂap?
The forearm ﬂap consists of skin from the inner surface of the forearm, above the wrist.
04-14-076.heading: What is a forearm ﬂap?

chunks:
How does the hand receive blood after surgery?
The radial artery is the blood vessel that supplies blood ﬂow to the forearm ﬂap, and it is removed with the ﬂap during surgery. Once this is removed, the ulnar artery is the only vessel supplying blood to the hand.
04-14-077.heading: How does the hand receive blood after surgery?

chunks:
How do we make sure its safe?
To ensure the hand will be safe and have sufﬁcient blood ﬂow after the ﬂap is taken, we do a simple, non-invasive test during the clinic examination. It is extremely rare to have an injury to the hand if this test looks good.
If there is doubt as to the safety of performing a radial forearm ﬂap, we will choose a different type of ﬂap instead.
04-14-078.heading: How do we make sure its safe?

chunks:
Is any bone taken from my arm?
Occasionally, bone is needed from the radius (forearm bone). This is not typical, and unless your surgeon has discussed this with you ahead of time it is extremely unlikely.
04-14-079.heading: Is any bone taken from my arm?

A drainage tube is left in the thigh at the time of surgery. This tube is about ¼" thick and is necessary to drain ﬂuid that accumulates in the thigh because of surgery. Usually, the drain stays in place for a couple of weeks and patients go home with this leg drain.

The nurses in the hospital will teach you how to care for your drain, which is an easy process. ●The drain needs to be emptied twice daily (or more frequently depending on the amount of drainage) and the output needs to be recorded. ●Your surgeon will want to know the daily

04-14-092.heading: When can I get my drain removed?

Occasionally, ﬂuid continues to accumulate even after the drain is removed. This can lead to swelling of the leg that feels soft, like a water balloon. When you stand up the swelling will move down to above the knee.

04-14-093.heading: What if there is still ﬂuid post-drain removal?

How will the ﬂuid (seroma) be drained?
The skin overlying the area is usually numb from the surgery and the ﬂuid can be drained through a small needle inserted through the skin. Sometimes this can require several drainage procedures if the ﬂuid keeps reaccumulating.
This is not urgent – you do not need to come in the same day for this problem. Waiting even a week or two will be ok. The procedure is very minor and not bothersome for patients.

Day of Surgery - Arrival
You will be asked to come to the hospital early in the morning. The hospital will call you the evening before surgery to tell you where to go and when to arrive. Usually, they want you to come in around 5:30 AM.
• This is to prepare you for anesthesia.
You will see the surgeons and anesthesiologists before going back to the operating room.
04-14-120.heading: Day of Surgery - Arrival

Day of Surgery – Start of Surgery
Once in the operating room you will undergo anesthesia. This takes 15-20 minutes. Then once you are asleep, we will prepare you for the surgery by padding and positioning your body, inserting a catheter into the bladder, and inserting several more IV lines.
Then the surgical site will be cleaned with antiseptics.
04-14-121.heading: Day of Surgery – Start of Surgery

Day of Surgery – During Surgery
By the time we start the operation, it will be around 8:30. Depending on the surgery, it may be anywhere from 5 to 12 or more hours.

After the procedure is completed, you will be transferred to the ICU and will wake up slowly. You may not remember anything from the night immediately following surgery.

04-14-124.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Hospital Stay

The main purpose of the length of stay is to make sure the surgical sites are healing and that the ﬂap is healthy. Wound healing problems often do not arise until about 1 week after surgery. This is the main reason patients remain in the hospital so long.

Fistula and Wound Infection
When you have surgery involving the mouth or throat, the wound is exposed to saliva. Even if the wounds are sutured perfectly, the body needs to take over and heal the wound or it will eventually open again.
Wound healing is more difﬁcult in the presence of saliva, but there is no way to keep it off of the wound.
04-14-130.heading: Fistula and Wound Infection

chunks:
Complications
If part of the incision opens, saliva can track into the incision and down into the neck. This is called a ﬁstula and can cause infection. If saliva is draining into blood vessels, it can cause them to clot or rupture, which can damage or kill a ﬂap.

Usually, a ﬁstula does not occur until about 7-10 days after surgery.
• If it does happen, we may simply watch it closely (if it is small) or it may require additional procedures to clean the wound, patch the leak or place new drains.
04-14-131.heading: Complications

chunks:
Flap Clotting
A clot can form in the blood vessel feeding the ﬂap and kill the ﬂap. While this is not the type of clot that can go to your lungs or brain and be life threatening, it can necessitate more surgery. Luckily, this is rare and occurs in about 1 patient out of every 100 cases.
04-14-132.heading: Flap Clotting

chunks:
Flap Clotting
Spontaneous ﬂap clotting is most common the ﬁrst couple days after surgery. After this it is rare unless there is a ﬁstula or infection around the ﬂap vessels, so the risk increases again about a week after surgery, when ﬁstulas and infections tend to develop.
04-14-133.heading: Flap Clotting

chunks:
Flap Clotting Risks
The risks may be higher if you have a condition that leads to blood clotting. ●Make sure your surgeon knows if you have ever had a blood clot in your legs or lungs or if blood clots run in your family. ●Clotting disorders include Factor V Leiden, Prothrombin
mutation, Protein C or S deﬁciency, elevated homocysteine, dysﬁbrinogenemia, and others. These are all rare but very important to know about.
04-14-134.heading: Flap Clotting Risks

chunks:
Flap Checks
Flap checks are done to assess the blood ﬂow to the ﬂap and make sure the ﬂap is alive and healthy. A ﬂap check involves looking at the ﬂap skin to make sure it the appropriate color.
• The skin should look like normal healthy skin.
• If it is very dark or purple or extremely
pale, this can be an indication of a problem.
04-14-135.heading: Flap Checks

chunks:
Flap Checks
A doppler stethoscope is also used to assess blood ﬂow to the ﬂap. This is a non-invasive way to listen to the pulsation of blood through the ﬂap. Sometimes we will need to scratch the ﬂap with a needle to assess the blood ﬂow to the ﬂap.
When this is done you will not feel pain from the needle stick because the ﬂap has no sensation as it has been detached from all nerves.

We recommend you quit smoking immediately after your cancer diagnosis and as many weeks as possible before the start of cancer treatment.
