chunks:
Why should I quit smoking immediately after a cancer diagnosis?
Smoking before surgery increases the risk of wound healing problems and death around the time of surgery. This is because quitting smoking improves your body’s ability to heal and respond to treatment.

chunks:
Why should I quit smoking immediately after a cancer diagnosis?

Why should I quit smoking immediately after a cancer diagnosis?
Quitting at the time of diagnosis may reduce the risk of your cancer returning after treatment. Quitting also reduces your risk that a second cancer will develop. Quitting smoking reduces your risk that your cancer will be fatal.

• Alcohol acts as a depressant in the body, affecting heart rate, blood pressure and breathing.

• Longer and more frequent hospitalizations
• Longer recoveries from treatment
05-01-17.heading: Why should I decrease my alcohol use?

Quitting alcohol helps your body ﬁght cancer and reduces your risk of developing new cancers. Quitting alcohol also reduces the severity of treatment side effects, such as mucositis.

05-01-19.heading: What to Expect When Quitting Alcohol

Why Do I Need Proper Nutrition?
Proper nutrition plays an important role before and after your surgery. Proper nutrition:
• Supports wound healing
• Strengthens your immune system
• Helps the body manage the stress of surgery
Malnutrition can increase the risk of complications, prolonged hospital stays, and slower recovery
05-01-22.heading: Why Do I Need Proper Nutrition?

chunks:
How do I maintain my nutrition status?
A dietician is a healthcare professional that specializes in food and nutrition. Ask your provider to place a referral if you would like to be contacted or need help with any of the following listed below. Their goals are to help you make sure you are:

• Consuming adequate protein
• Maintaining your weight
• Staying hydrated They can also help with:
• Coping with potential nutrition-related side effects from treatment.
• Tube feeding assistance. For more information, refer to the NG tube module.
05-01-23.heading: How do I maintain my nutrition status?

chunks:
How do I maintain my nutrition status?
Protein is essential for faster healing so it’s important to increase your protein intake both before and after surgery. Calories are equally important for the healing process as they help you maintain your weight.
• Select foods that are both high in protein and calories to support recovery.

• Drink 2-3 protein shakes a day for at least two weeks prior to surgery is recommended. Shakes that are high in protein and calories are best. For more information on speciﬁc brands, refer to the Dietician Orientation video at the start of this module.
05-01-24.heading: How do I maintain my nutrition status?

chunks:
What are good sources of protein?
Depending on tumor size and location, soft protein sources may be easier for you to eat before surgery. After surgery you will likely rely on soft foods, soups, and shakes for your protein needs.
Eggs are a good source of protein. You can incorporate dishes like egg salad, quiche, and custard into your diet.
05-01-25.heading: What are good sources of protein?

chunks:
What are good sources of protein?
Meat is also a good source of protein: include meats such as chicken, pork, beef, and lamb to meet your protein needs.
• If it is difﬁcult to chew or swallow meat, opt for shredded or ground meat with extra gravy, or choose casseroles and chicken salad for easier consumption.
Fish is another great soft high protein food.
05-01-26.heading: What are good sources of protein?

What are good sources of protein?

• Choosing whole milk or chocolate milk can add extra calories, helping you maintain your weight.
• For added calories and protein, you can prepare oatmeal with milk instead of water
• Creamy or chunky soup like clam chowder, potato, cream of chicken, broccoli, or soups with beans are also a good option.
05-01-27.heading: What are good sources of protein?

Staying active before surgery can help your body prepare and recover more quickly. Generally, healthy, active people regain full mobility quicker than patients who have a lower baseline level of mobility and activity prior to surgery.

What To Expect When You Wake Up
When you wake up, you will be coming out of a major surgery and still feeling the effects of anesthesia. This is completely normal. You will be given pain medication to keep you comfortable but it may also make you feel groggy, sleepy, or a little confused at ﬁrst.
You will likely rely on your caregivers or written or text-based forms of communication, at ﬁrst.
05-02-08.heading: What To Expect When You Wake Up

chunks:
What To Expect When You Wake Up
When you wake up from surgery, you will likely have several thing attached to your body, such as a tracheostomy, drains, tubes, or monitors.
• These are all in place to help you heal and will be removed as you recover.
It is helpful to remember that the ﬁrst few days after surgery can be the hardest to adjust to but your team is there to support you through this difﬁcult experience.
05-02-09.heading: What To Expect When You Wake Up

chunks:
Will I be able to eat and drink?
Because your surgery involves the head and neck, you won't be able to eat or drink by mouth when you wake up. Your care team will ensure you receive nutrition in other ways until your surgeon determines that it is safe for you to resume eating and drinking again.
05-02-10.heading: Will I be able to eat and drink?

chunks:
How independent will I be after surgery?
At the beginning, you will need help from the hospital staff to do most things--this is completely normal and expected. You may also need to rely on your caretaker during this time to communicate your needs.
• Having someone who knows you well can be comforting and can help ensure your care team understands your wishes.
05-02-11.heading: How independent will I be after surgery?

chunks:
How independent will I be after surgery?
You will be moving around and encouraged to get out of bed the ﬁrst few days with assistance. During your stay, you will gradually regain strength and be able to move around more on your own, but this won’t happen right away.
Your care team will be there to support you every step of the way. This team includes physical and occupational therapy.
05-02-12.heading: How independent will I be after surgery?

chunks:
What to Expect in the ICU
When you ﬁrst wake up from the surgery, you will be placed in the Surgical Intensive Care Unit (SICU). In the SICU you will have your own room with glass doors that can be closed for privacy and to maintain a quiet environment.

There is a lot of activity in the SICU and a lot of people coming to check on various aspects of your healing.
• After your reconstruction, your team will be monitoring your new free ﬂap frequently to make sure your new tissue is healthy and healing.
05-02-14.heading: What to Expect in the ICU

chunks:
What to Expect in the ICU
The ﬁrst few nights in the ICU may not provide quality restful sleep. It is important to ensure you have items that will make you as comfortable as you can be.
05-02-15.heading: What to Expect in the ICU

chunks:
Comfort Care in the SICU
In the SICU, your pain medication will likely be given through a device called a Patient-Controlled Analgesia (PCA) pump also known as a “pain button”.
• This device allows you to self-administer medication for pain relief by pressing a button.

If you are tall or you ﬁnd that your feet touch the headboard, the hospital can provide a bed extender.
• You can also ask you care team ahead of time if you think you might need one.
05-02-16.heading: Comfort Care in the SICU

chunks:
Can I have visitors in the ICU?
Yes, you can have visitors in the ICU. Check with the front desk to ﬁnd out the visitor policy.
05-02-17.heading: Can I have visitors in the ICU?

chunks:
What to Expect on the Recovery Floor
After a few days, you will be transferred from the ICU to a recovery ﬂoor. Here you will have a private room (with a full bath) with doors that can be closed for privacy and to maintain a quiet environment. There is less activity here as well.
• While your care team will still be monitoring your healing, it will be less frequent than in the ICU.
05-02-19.heading: What to Expect on the Recovery Floor

chunks:
What to Expect on the Recovery Floor
On the ﬂoor, your pain medication will likely be given PRN which means as needed.
• This means your pain medication will not be given at set times, but instead when you ask for it. This gives you more control over when you receive pain relief.

• It is important to pay attention to how you are feeling and let your care team when you are feeling uncomfortable. Don’t wait until the pain is severe--your team is here to help manage your pain and keep you as comfortable as possible.
05-02-20.heading: What to Expect on the Recovery Floor

chunks:
Planning for Discharge
As you get closer to leaving the hospital, a care coordinator will help ensure everything is in place for a smooth and safe discharge. They work closely with your doctors, nurses, and caregiver to:

• Coordinate arrangements following your discharge including medical equipment, prescriptions, nutritional supplements.
• Answer any questions you have about your discharge plan.
05-02-22.heading: Planning for Discharge

chunks:
Where will I discharge to?
When it's time to leave the hospital, your care team and care coordinator will talk with you and your loved ones to help choose the best option for your recovery. Common discharge options include:
• Home with home health
• To a nursing facility
• To a rehabilitation facility
More information about each of these discharge options will be provided on the next slides.
05-02-23.heading: Where will I discharge to?

chunks:
Where will I discharge to?
Home with home health:
• You go home but have a home health provider visit you a few times a week to help with things like wound care and medications.
05-02-24.heading: Where will I discharge to?

chunks:
Where will I discharge to?
To a rehabilitation facility:
• You go to a rehab center for more intensive therapy, like physical or occupational therapy, to help you recover strength and function before returning home. To a skilled nursing facility:
• You temporarily stay at a facility where you can get more hands-on medical care and help with daily activities until you are stronger.
05-02-25.heading: Where will I discharge to?

chunks:
Planning for Discharge
Before you leave the hospital, your care team will help you schedule follow-up appointments with your treatment team before you discharge.
• You will be coming back in about a week for a follow up appointment with your surgical oncologist and your reconstructive surgeon.
05-02-26.heading: Planning for Discharge

chunks:
Planning for Discharge
Should you go home with any medical equipment your hospital team will provide education on the items you will discharge with.
• This may include things like tracheostomy training, wound vac training, wound care training, feeding tube training.
05-02-27.heading: Planning for Discharge

chunks:
Support at Home
If possible, after you leave the hospital, having help from a caregiver or loved one will be very important. Caregivers are encouraged to reach out to the care coordinator if any questions arise.
They can assist with daily tasks, help manage medications, and provide emotional support as you continue to recover at home.

If you have any questions or concerns at any point, don’t hesitate to talk with your care team—they’re here to help and support you throughout your recovery. Additionally, caregivers can contact the care coordinator if they have any questions.

What is a Modiﬁed Barium Swallow Study (MBS)?
A modiﬁed barium swallow study is a video X-ray that shows how food and drink move through your mouth and throat when you swallow. It helps check how well your throat muscles are working and how food travels into the top part of your esophagus (food pipe). It speciﬁcally tests the safety and efﬁciency of your swallow.
05-03-2.heading: What is a Modiﬁed Barium Swallow Study (MBS)?

chunks:
What is the Process of getting an MBS?
During testing, you will be seated in an open x-ray machine. Video x-rays are recorded as you swallow liquid and bites of food. The food and drink you consume is tinted with barium, which allows it to be seen under an x-ray.
05-03-3.heading: What is the Process of getting an MBS?

chunks:
What Happens if you have Difﬁculty Swallowing?
The MBS study helps your care team ﬁgure out which foods and drinks are safe for you to eat. It also lets the speech pathologist see if you might beneﬁt from swallowing therapy.
Having this test done before head and neck cancer treatment can help your team plan for your nutrition and decide if a feeding tube may be needed after treatment.
05-03-4.heading: What Happens if you have Difﬁculty Swallowing?

chunks:
How Should You Prepare for the Test?
• You can eat and drink normally before the test; there are no restrictions.
• Bring any food or drink you ﬁnd hard to swallow so we can observe you ingesting them.
• Avoid wearing jewelry or clothing with metal.
• If you use special drinking tools (like a straw or bottle), please bring them.

What is a Tracheostomy Tube?
A tracheostomy tube is a medical device inserted into a small opening in your neck called a stoma, which leads directly into your windpipe (trachea).

This tube helps you breathe when you're unable to breathe normally through your nose or mouth. It allows air to ﬂow directly into your lungs and may be used temporarily or long-term depending on your condition.

Parts of Your Tracheostomy Tube
The inner cannula is a hollow tube placed in the tracheostomy opening that remains there during routine use. It's primary purpose is to keep the airway open and allows it to be cleaned at regular intervals without removing the tracheostomy tube.

Protecting Your Tracheostomy Tube
Do not let water get into your tracheostomy tube. This means no swimming or water sports.

When you take a shower, move the shower head, so the water hits you below the tracheostomy tube. When you rinse your head or neck, cup your hands over your tracheostomy tube. You can also wring out a washcloth and put it over your tracheostomy tube.

Protecting Your Tracheostomy Tube
Protect the opening of the tracheostomy tube. You can do this with a piece of moist gauze, knitted tracheostomy cover, or folded handkerchief. This is important so things like dust, hair, lint, or insects cannot get into your tracheostomy tube.
06-03-11.heading: Protecting Your Tracheostomy Tube Continued

Improving Comfort for Your Tracheostomy Tube
Take in plenty of liquids either by mouth or feeding tube once the clinical team has deemed it safe. This helps keep your mucus thinner and easier to cough out.

Humidifying the Airway
Humidiﬁcation helps keep your secretions thin, which reduces the risk of developing mucus plugs. Wear your tracheostomy mask (also known as tracheostomy collar) while sleeping or when sitting at home for long periods of time.

Humidifying the Airway
Both tracheostomy masks and HME caps provide humidiﬁcation of the airway. A tracheostomy mask or tracheostomy collar provides external humidiﬁed air or oxygen through mist.

What is a gastrostomy (G tube) or nasogastric tube (NG tube)?
A gastrostomy tube (G tube) and a nasogastric tube (NG tube) are types of feeding tubes that help provide nutrition, ﬂuids, and medications when a person is unable to eat or drink enough by mouth.
They are essential tools for supporting health and healing in people with certain medical conditions affecting the mouth, throat, esophagus, or digestive system.
07-01-2.heading: What is a gastrostomy (G tube) or nasogastric tube (NG tube)?

chunks:
What is a gastrostomy tube (G tube)?
A G tube is a soft, ﬂexible tube that is placed through the skin of the abdomen directly into the stomach. It provides a way to deliver nutrition, ﬂuids, and medications directly into the stomach when oral feeding is not possible or safe.
G tubes are typically used for long-term feeding needs (weeks to years). Source: Cancer Research UK / Wikimedia Commons
07-01-3.heading: What is a gastrostomy tube (G tube)?

chunks:
What is a nasogastric tube (NG tube)?
An NG tube is a thin, ﬂexible tube that is inserted through the nose, down the throat, and into the stomach. NG tubes are generally used for short-term feeding (days to weeks). They may also be used to remove stomach contents or administer medications.
Source: Cancer Research UK / Wikimedia Commons
07-01-4.heading: What is a nasogastric tube (NG tube)?

chunks:
Parts of the G tube or NG tube
1. Feeding tube - soft tube inserted into the stomach (G tube) or through the nose (NG tube) 2. External Flange/Bumper- Round disk on the outside of the body that holds the tube in place 3. Internal Retention Device- Internal balloon or bumper that prevents the tube from slipping out
07-01-5.heading: Parts of the G tube or NG tube

chunks:
Parts of the G tube or NG tube
4. Extension set- connects to the feeding tube and allows for feeding or ﬂushing 5. Feeding bag/ syringe- holds liquid nutrition or medication to be given through the tube 6. Cap or clamp- closes off the tube when not in use, preventing leakage or air entry
7. Stoma - the small opening on your body’s surface where a feeding tube (like a G tube or NG tube) enters and connects to your stomach or digestive system.
07-01-6.heading: Parts of the G tube or NG tube Continued

Day 1–7 Post-Insertion
Clean around the tube and stoma (hole where the tube goes through the belly into the stomach) with mild soap and water using gauze or Q-tips. Dry thoroughly and place a new piece of gauze with a Y cut into the center to allow for the gauze to sit around the tube and under the external ﬂange.
Do not use lotions, ointments, or creams on the skin. Change the gauze at least every 24 hours.

I Can Manage Cancer After Day 7 Post-Insertion

After Day 7 Post-Insertion
After cleaning the tube and stoma site, rotate or spin the tube in your hand several times, this is to make sure it is free and can freely spin. If it does not rotate or spin, please call the clinic.
Rotate the tube 360° once daily to prevent sticking. Rotate the ﬂange/bumper feet at least once a day so that the feet do not rest on the same area of skin as this can cause damage.
07-02-05.heading: After Day 7 Post-Insertion Continued

If you still have the stitch on the tube, please call the clinic to schedule an appointment to have this removed.

Nutritional Supplement Information
Before you leave the hospital, you and your family will be taught how to use your feeding tube. It’s important to feel comfortable using it at home. The tube is used to give you liquid nutrition, but you can also use it for other liquids like water or electrolyte drinks.
It is important to administer the nutritional supplement slowly. Do not to rush the feeding as it can cause an upset stomach.
07-02-07.heading: Nutritional Supplement Information

chunks:
Checking Your G Tube Position
Your G tube has a number printed on it near the plastic disk that rests against your skin (called the external bumper or ﬂange). This number shows how far the tube is inserted. When you ﬁrst got your tube, the doctor or nurse made a note of this number—it’s your correct tube position.
Check this number every day. The number should stay the same unless your healthcare provider tells you otherwise.
07-02-09.heading: Checking Your G Tube Position

chunks:
Checking Your G Tube Position
If the number is smaller, the tube may have pulled out. Please call the clinic immediately. If the number is larger, this may cause the tube to be too loose. To correct this, gently pull the tube up and slide the external ﬂange down to the correct marking.
07-02-10.heading: Checking Your G Tube Position Continued

chunks:
G Tube Daily Care
The external ﬂange/bumper on the G tube should rest snugly on top of the skin, but there should be enough room for daily cleaning underneath. After the G tube is inserted, there may be a small amount of red or yellowish ﬂuid around the new site. This is normal.
07-02-11.heading: G Tube Daily Care

chunks:
G-Tube Daily Care
Mild leakage around the tube is normal. The leakage might be the color of the tube feeds, stomach/bilious ﬂuid or pinkish.

Place a new piece of gauze with a Y cut into the center to allow for the gauze to sit around the tube and under the external ﬂange. Change this as the gauze gets saturated. DO NOT allow saturated gauze to sit on your skin for any period of time.
07-02-12.heading: G-Tube Daily Care Continued

chunks:
G-Tube Daily Care
Keep the tube at a 90° angle from the skin for the ﬁrst 2 weeks. This will help prevent leaking and other complications. Tuck at least 1 inch of gauze around the tube and on top of the bumper, and tape the gauze in place. Do not tape the tube itself down to the skin.
07-02-13.heading: G-Tube Daily Care Continued

chunks:
Chemical Burns
If the skin turns red or is hot, then please call the clinic and upload a picture of the site on MyChart. This is usually a chemical burn from the drainage around the tube, if this is conﬁrmed, then follow the following steps:
- Keep the site as dry as possible, even if this means replacing the gauze frequently. - Place a thin layer of diaper rash cream on the skin around the tube site to protect it from drainage.
07-02-14.heading: Chemical Burns

chunks:
Showering
You may shower 48 hours after tube insertion. You may NOT submerge your tube site (in a bathtub/swimming pool/lake/etc.) until at least 2 weeks after insertion. It is important to cleanse the site with mild soapy water and thoroughly dry the site after it gets wet.
07-02-15.heading: Showering

chunks:
G-Tube Maintenance
Flush your tube with 30 mL of drinking water: - Before and after feedings - Before and after medications Regular ﬂushing will help to prevent the tube from clogging. If any feeding or medication is left in the tube, this puts your tube at a high risk of clogging.
Some discoloration of the G-tube over time is normal.
07-02-16.heading: G-Tube Maintenance

chunks:
Replacing Your G-Tube
Replace your G-tube approximately every 6 months, or sooner if damaged. Please call the clinic for an appointment to replace your tube. If the tube cracks or the connections come loose sooner, please call the clinic for a replacement sooner.
07-02-17.heading: Replacing Your G-Tube

chunks:
Oral Care
It is important to maintain good oral care even if you may not be eating/drinking anything by mouth. This can help prevent complications like infection.

Please gently brush your teeth, gums, tongue, and palate at least twice a day if you have been told it is safe to do so. You should also rinse with mouthwash if it is deemed safe (Biotene can help if you are experiencing dry mouth).
07-02-18.heading: Oral Care

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Oral Care
If you are at a high risk of aspiration, you may need to use oral swabs and a suction catheter.
07-02-19.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Oral Care

chunks:
If Your Tube is Clogged
If you are unable to ﬂush your tube or meet signiﬁcant resistance when trying to ﬂush, your tube is likely clogged. Don’t panic! Here are a few things you can try to unclog your tube:
- Make sure your tube is not clamped - If using a valve at the end of your tube, make sure it is in the correct position
07-02-21.heading: If Your Tube is Clogged

chunks:
If Your Tube is Clogged
- Carefully massage the tube between your thumb and index ﬁnger to try to break up any clogs. Be careful not to tug or pull hard on your tube to keep it in place. - Hook up an empty syringe and slowly and gently try to draw back any material that is stuck.
07-02-22.heading: If Your Tube is Clogged Continued

chunks:
If Your Tube is Clogged
Try using warm water to unclog the tube. Use water that is hot but not too hot—it should be warm enough to drink comfortably. Gently push the warm water into the tube and let it sit for 10 to 15 minutes. Then, try ﬂushing the tube again. If you still encounter resistance, repeat the process:
- Add more warm water - Gently massage the tube - Wait another 10 to 15 minutes Keep trying until the tube ﬂushes easily.
07-02-23.heading: If Your Tube is Clogged Continued

chunks:
If Your Tube is Clogged
If your tube remains clogged after attempting the 6 steps described previously, you should present to the emergency room to either let medical professionals attempt to unclog it or have the tube exchanged.
07-02-24.heading: If Your Tube is Clogged Continued

chunks:
If Your Tube is Clogged
Do NOT try to ﬂush your tube with a large amount of force. This can cause the tubing to bubble and even burst or leak. If you notice that your tube is leaking (not from your skin but from the actual tubing itself) you will need to have your tube replaced.
Do NOT attempt to insert anything into your tube to mechanically push the clog out. This is likely to damage the tube and is not safe.
07-02-25.heading: If Your Tube is Clogged Continued

chunks:
Emergency Situations
If your tube comes out within 4 weeks of placement, go to the ER immediately. The hole can close within hours. Call the UTSW MDSC Surgery Clinic at 214-645-2900 and/or the on-call surgeon for instructions. This is an emergency. Do not wait until morning.
07-02-26.heading: Emergency Situations

chunks:
The Nasogastric (NG) Tube
• The NG tube is used to deliver nutrients from the nose to the stomach.
• If the tube is only needed for shorter periods of time, the NG tube is usually preferred over the G tube. Source: Cancer Research UK / Wikimedia Commons
07-03-02.heading: The Nasogastric (NG) Tube

chunks:
How is the NG tube secured?
• Often a nasal bridle system is used to secure the NG tube. The system has small magnets to help keep the tube in the nose, which should not be painful.
• This decreases risk of accidental removal including during feedings. However, if the bridle is pulled this may result in discomfort.
07-03-03.heading: How is the NG tube secured?

chunks:
Nutritional Supplement Information
• Before you leave the hospital, you and your family will be taught how to use your feeding tube. It’s important to feel comfortable using it at home.
• The tube is used to give you liquid nutrition, but you can also use it for other liquids like water or electrolyte drinks.
• It is important to administer the nutritional supplement slowly. Do not to rush the feeding as it can cause an upset stomach.
07-03-04.heading: Nutritional Supplement Information

chunks:
How Tube Feeds Are Delivered
• Bolus feeds: Formula is given manually using a syringe several times per day.
• Pump feeds: Formula is delivered slowly using a feeding pump (e.g., Kangaroo pump), often overnight.
• Your care team will choose the method based on your nutritional needs and comfort.
07-03-05.heading: How Tube Feeds Are Delivered

chunks:
NG Tube Clogs
• To help keep the tube working properly, try to avoid putting crushed-up medications or thick liquids through the tube, as these can cause clogs.
• If the tube does get clogged, a small amount of carbonated soda (like ginger ale or cola) may help clear it. If that doesn’t work, you may need to visit your doctor’s ofﬁce or the emergency room.
07-03-06.heading: NG Tube Clogs

chunks:
Comfort Tips for Nasogastric (NG) Tube Use
• Wearing a nasal feeding tube can feel uncomfortable at ﬁrst, and it’s common to become very aware of its presence.
• The tube may occasionally get tugged or caught on clothing or other objects. While it is unlikely to come out, accidental pulling can cause discomfort.
07-03-07.heading: Comfort Tips for Nasogastric (NG) Tube Use

chunks:
Comfort Tips for Nasogastric (NG) Tube Use
• To help manage this discomfort, some patients ﬁnd it helpful to secure the tube by gently pinning it to the collar of their shirt or by looping it up and around the ear to keep it out of the way.
• Finding a method that works for you can make daily activities more comfortable and help you feel more at ease while wearing the tube.
07-03-08.heading: Comfort Tips for Nasogastric (NG) Tube Use

chunks:
Removing the NG Tube
• When it’s time to remove the feeding tube, the process is quick and can be done during a scheduled clinic appointment.
• Removing the NG tube does not require a return to the hospital.
07-03-09.heading: Removing the NG Tube

chunks:
Warning signs (to contact your provider)
• Bright green output
• Bloody drainage
• Increased nausea/vomiting
• Sudden increase in suction output
07-03-10.heading: Warning signs (to contact your provider)

chunks:
Wound Care for Incisions
Incision: A surgical cut made by the doctor to access the treatment area, which is usually closed with stitches or staples. Dressings should be changed regularly to prevent infection of the wound site.
If the dressings are more complex, a home health nurse may be able to come to your home to change the dressings. Talk to your doctor about this option.
08-01-02.heading: Wound Care for Incisions

chunks:
How do I avoid irritating the incision area?
• Wear loose-ﬁtting clothing over the donor site.
• Avoid rubbing, soaking, or scrubbing the area
• Avoid bathtubs or pools
• Don’t expose it to direct sunlight because the skin is extra sensitive
08-01-03.heading: How do I avoid irritating the incision area?

chunks:
How to prevent infection?
• Wash your hands before touching the area.
• Don’t apply creams or ointments unless prescribed.
• Watch for signs of infection: ○ Increased redness or swelling ○ Yellow or green drainage ○ Foul smell ○ Fever or chills
08-01-04.heading: How to prevent infection?

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer When is pain concerning?
Pain is worrisome if it is continually increasing over several days. New or worsening pain at the incision or donor site is also worrisome.
08-01-05.heading: I Can Manage Cancer When is pain concerning?

chunks:
When should I be worried about swelling?
If swelling is gradually worsening over several consecutive days, this may be a cause for concern, especially if there is also redness of the neck or face.
08-01-06.heading: When should I be worried about swelling?

chunks:
When should I be worried about drainage?
New or foul smelling drainage is worrisome especially if you also have fever over 100.4°F (38°C). Cloudy drainage is is a warning sign as well. Talk to your surgical team.
08-01-07.heading: When should I be worried about drainage?

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer Saltwater Mouthwash
Saltwater mouth rinses are commonly recommended after many HNC surgeries to promote oral hygiene, reduce infection risk, and support healing.
08-01-08.heading: I Can Manage Cancer Saltwater Mouthwash

chunks:
When to use a saltwater mouthwash?
• Oral Cavity Surgeries: ○ Glossectomy (partial or total tongue removal) ○ Mandibulectomy ○ Maxillectomy ○ Oral composite resection ○ Mouth cancer surgery
• Pharyngectomy
• Laryngectomy (total or partial)
These surgeries involve direct incisions in the mouth. Saltwater rinses help keep wounds clean, reduce bacteria, and prevent infection without irritating the surgical site.
08-01-09.heading: When to use a saltwater mouthwash?

chunks:
How to use the mouthwash?
Supplies needed:
• 16 ounce bottle of water
• 1 teaspoon salt
• 1 teaspoon baking soda 1. Keep a bottle by the bathroom and kitchen sinks 2. Rinse, gargle, and spit after meals, before bed, and anytime your mouth feels dry or sore
08-01-10.heading: How to use the mouthwash?

chunks:
What is a donor site?
You have a skin graft donor site where a thin layer of skin was removed (a split-thickness skin graft) to help repair another area. Most commonly, the skin graft is taken from the thigh. The donor site may look like a rug burn or road rash—this is completely normal.
08-02-02.heading: What is a donor site?

chunks:
Understanding the Donor Site
Only the outermost layer of skin is removed. The full thickness of the skin (dermis) is not affected. Because the wound is very superﬁcial, it generally heals well with minimal risk of infection. If an infection does occur, it is usually very mild.
08-02-03.heading: Understanding the Donor Site

chunks:
Initial Dressing – Mepilex Ag
Your donor site has been covered with a dressing called Mepilex Ag, which contains silver to help prevent infection and promote healing. This dressing may look bloody or crusty over time. This is expected and normal.
08-02-04.heading: Initial Dressing – Mepilex Ag

chunks:
Caring for the Mepilex Ag Dressing
Keep the Mepilex Ag dressing in place until it falls off on its own. Do not remove it unless instructed to do so by your doctor. If the edges begin to peel up, you may trim them carefully with clean scissors
08-02-05.heading: Caring for the Mepilex Ag Dressing

chunks:
What to do if the Mepilex comes off early?
If the dressing comes off early or is removed, some bleeding may occur. Apply gentle pressure to stop any bleeding. This is not cause for concern.
08-02-06.heading: What to do if the Mepilex comes off early?

chunks:
What to do after the Mepilex comes off?
Once the Mepilex Ag dressing has naturally fallen off, begin daily dressing care as follows:

1. There is no speciﬁc need to clean the donor area. It is okay to shower and to let water run over the site. Do not scrub or soak the area. Pat it dry with a clean towel. Do not submerge it in a tub or pool. 2. Apply a thin layer of Vaseline or Aquaphor to the wound.
08-02-07.heading: What to do after the Mepilex comes off?

chunks:
What to do after the Mepilex comes off (continued)?
3. Cover the area with a non-adherent dressing, such as Vaseline gauze, Adaptid, Xeroform, or Telfa.

4. Place a layer of regular gauze over the non-adherent dressing and tape it down. Do not place regular gauze directly on the wound, as it may stick and cause bleeding when removed. 5. Change the dressing once per day, or more often if it becomes wet or dirty or develops an odor.
6. If the dressing starts to stick to the wound, add more Vaseline or Aquaphor to keep the area moist.
08-02-08.heading: What to do after the Mepilex comes off (continued)?

chunks:
What to expect during healing?
Some bleeding is normal, especially during dressing changes, because the healing tissue is very delicate. If bleeding occurs:
• Apply ﬁrm pressure with the dressing material for several minutes.
• You may also use gauze ﬂuffs and secure them with gentle pressure using tape.
08-02-09.heading: What to expect during healing?

chunks:
How do I know the wound is healed?
The wound is considered healed when a new layer of skin has formed and there is no longer any crusting or scabbing.

The new skin is usually pink or purple in color and may look different or shinier from the surrounding skin at ﬁrst. This is normal, and the color will even out over time. Most donor sites heal within 2-3 weeks
08-02-10.heading: How do I know the wound is healed?

chunks:
How do I care for the new skin after healing is complete?
Once healed, the new skin is more fragile and can bleed if scratched or rubbed. While a dressing is no longer needed, you may keep it covered with an ACE bandage or gauze if it is sensitive.
You may apply a non-adherent dressing with gentle pressure if any minor bleeding occurs.
08-02-11.heading: How do I care for the new skin after healing is complete?

chunks:
Long-term Skin Care
After new skin has formed, you may begin applying vitamin E lotion or other over-the-counter scar cream to help with the appearance of the scar. The new skin should be protected from direct sunlight to reduce the chance of discoloration. This is especially true during the ﬁrst year.
You may use sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher) on the area once the skin has completely healed. Do not submerge the area in bathtubs, swimming pools, lakes, or hot tubs until the new skin has fully formed.
08-02-12.heading: Long-term Skin Care

chunks:
What is a drain tube?
A drainage tube is left in the surgical wound at the time of surgery. This tube is about ¼" thick and is necessary to drain ﬂuid that accumulates because of surgery. Usually, the drain stays in place for a couple of weeks and patients go home with this drain. drain tube
08-03-2.heading: What is a drain tube?

chunks:
How do I take care of my drain?
The drain needs to be emptied twice daily (or more depending on the amount of drainage) and the output needs to be recorded. The surgeon will want to know the daily output of the drain in milliliters (ML) for each 24-hour period.
When the drain output is less than 30-50 ML per 24-hour period, it may be ready to be removed.
08-03-3.heading: How do I take care of my drain?

chunks:
Will ﬂuid accumulate after the drain tube is removed?
Occasionally, ﬂuid continues to accumulate even after the drain is removed. This can lead to swelling of the skin that feels soft, like a water balloon. When you stand up the swelling will drift down to the lowest portion of the surgical site.
08-03-4.heading: Will ﬂuid accumulate after the drain tube is removed?

chunks:
What should I do if ﬂuid accumulates after the drain is removed?
This ﬂuid (called a seroma) usually needs to be drained but the procedure is easy and usually done in the ofﬁce.

The skin overlying the area is usually numb from the surgery and the ﬂuid can be drained through a small needle inserted through the skin. Sometimes this can require several drainage procedures if the ﬂuid keeps reaccumulating.
08-03-5.heading: What should I do if ﬂuid accumulates after the drain is removed?

chunks:
How long can I wait to get the ﬂuid drained?
This is not urgent – you do not need to come in the same day for this problem. Waiting even a week or two will be okay
08-03-6.heading: How long can I wait to get the ﬂuid drained?

chunks:
What is a wound VAC ?
A Wound VAC (Vacuum-Assisted Closure) is a medical device that supports wound healing through negative pressure therapy. This increases blood ﬂow in the wound and helps with healing.
08-04-2.heading: What is a wound VAC ?

chunks:
How does it work?
It involves placing a foam dressing within the wound bed, sealing the area with an adhesive drape, and connecting it to a vacuum pump via tubing. The system gently removes ﬂuid and debris, reduces swelling, and helps draw the edges of the wound together.
08-04-3.heading: How does it work?

chunks:
Why use a wound VAC?
Wound VACs are commonly used after major head and neck cancer surgeries, especially when there are large or complex surgical wounds, tissue ﬂaps, or areas at high risk for ﬂuid collection.
They help the area heal by removing ﬂuid, improving blood ﬂow, preventing infection, and protecting tissue ﬂaps.
08-04-4.heading: Why use a wound VAC?

chunks:
What to expect?
The VAC device will remain in place continuously, typically connected to portable suction. The dressing is sealed tightly to the skin, and you may feel a light pulling or suction sensation. Mild discomfort can occur but should not be severe.
The dressing is usually changed every 2–3 days by trained providers, either in the hospital or clinic setting.
08-04-5.heading: What to expect?

chunks:
Daily management of the Wound VAC
Avoid disconnecting or turning off the Wound VAC unless instructed. Keep the tubing free of kinks and below the wound site to allow proper drainage.
08-04-6.heading: Daily management of the Wound VAC

chunks:
When to Call Your Care Team
Make sure the seal is intact—if you hear air leaks or see dressing lifting, notify your care team. If the canister becomes full or alarms sound, contact your provider or home health nurse.
08-04-7.heading: When to Call Your Care Team

chunks:
Hygiene and activity precautions
• Do not shower while the VAC is in place unless your provider has approved a special cover or dressing.
• Avoid submerging the VAC or dressing in water.
• Be cautious with neck movement and avoid pulling on the tubing.
• Limit strenuous activities and avoid laying directly on the VAC dressing site to prevent pressure disruption.
08-04-8.heading: Hygiene and activity precautions

chunks:
I Can Manage Cancer What is cancer-related Lymphedema
• Lymphedema refers to swelling caused by the buildup of lymph ﬂuid beneath the skin. The lymphatic system normally functions to collect and transport excess ﬂuid, proteins, and waste products from body tissues back into the bloodstream. It also plays a key role in ﬁltering out bacteria, viruses, and other harmful substances.
• When lymph nodes or vessels are damaged or obstructed, lymph ﬂuid cannot drain effectively. This results in ﬂuid accumulation and swelling.
08-05-2.heading: I Can Manage Cancer What is cancer-related Lymphedema

chunks:
What are the causes?
Cancer related lymphedema occurs when the lymphatic system is blocked or damaged from the effects of cancer cancer treatments. Common causes:
• Surgery to remove lymph nodes
• Radiation treatment for cancer
• Tumor growth from cancer
08-05-3.heading: What are the causes?

chunks:
What increases the risk?
The following factors may make you more likely to develop this complication:
• Older age
• Obesity
• Rheumatoid or inﬂammatory arthritis
• History of lymphedema
08-05-4.heading: What increases the risk?

chunks:
What are the physical exam signs of lymphedema?
• Sensation of heaviness, tightness, or fullness in the affected area
• Mild swelling that may come and go, especially at the end of the day
• Clothing, jewelry, or compression garments feeling tighter than usual
• Skin changes, such as slight pufﬁness, decreased elasticity, or indentation when pressed
• Aching, tingling, or discomfort in the limb or region
• Reduced range of motion in the neck, shoulder, or affected limb
08-05-5.heading: What are the physical exam signs of lymphedema?

chunks:
How to treat lymphedema?
Compression Garments
• Sleeves or stockings to maintain pressure
• Elevated the limb above the level of your heart if possible Compression Bandaging
• Multi-layer wraps to reduce swelling Pneumatic Compression Pump

• External pump with inﬂatable sleeve to promote drainage Surgery (for severe cases)
• Reserved for chronic, refractory lymphedema Complete Decongestive Therapy (CDT)
• Manual lymphatic drainage (specialized massage)
• Compression therapy
• Gentle exercise
• Skin care
08-05-6.heading: How to treat lymphedema?

chunks:
Instructions at home
DO DON’T

• Check your skin and the affected area everyday for signs of increased swelling, irritation or redness
• Keep the affected area clean and dry
• Apply lotion to prevent dry skin
• Protect your skin from cuts and injuries
• Protect the affected area from extreme cold
• Avoid medical procedures such as blood draws and injections in the affected limb

• Walk barefoot
• Have your blood pressure checked on the affected limb
• Apply ice to the affected area
• Use a heating pad over the affected area
• Wear right clothes, shoes, or jewelry
• Sit with your legs crossed
08-05-7.heading: Instructions at home

chunks:
Contact a healthcare provider IF….
• You have a fever
• You have a cut or injury that does not heal
• You have redness or pain in the affected area
• You have new or increased swelling
• You develop purplish spots or sores on your affected limb
08-05-8.heading: Contact a healthcare provider IF….

chunks:
Seek immediate medical attention IF…..
• You develop a skin rash
• You have chills or sweating
• You have trouble breathing
08-05-9.heading: Seek immediate medical attention IF…..

08-06-03.heading: Dysphagia Strategies and

chunks:
What is Dysphagia?
• Dysphagia, or difﬁculty swallowing, is a common postoperative symptom.
• Postoperative dysphagia can result from swelling, nerve irritation, muscle weakness, or structural changes that disrupt the normal swallowing mechanism.
08-06-04.heading: What is Dysphagia?

chunks:
Speech Therapy
• Speech therapy plays an integral role in your ability to swallow and is essential to optimize your health while undergoing treatment
• A wide range of conditions, illnesses, and their treatments can disrupt the process of swallowing which can lead to choking, malnutrition, and other problems
• UTSW Speech Therapy department will provide you more strategies to successfully navigate your nutritional status before and after surgery.
08-06-05.heading: Speech Therapy

chunks:
Exercise #1: Jaw Resistance
1. Slightly open your mouth and press chin against the palm 2. Let your elbow be on your knee 3. Feel the engagement in the center neck and below the chin 4. Sustain the position for 10 seconds 5. Keep breathing (5 repetitions, 3-5 times a day)
08-06-06.heading: Exercise #1: Jaw Resistance

chunks:
Exercise #2: Tongue Hold (Masako)
1. Hold your tongue between your teeth 2. Swallow while keeping your tongue between your teeth This exercise strengthens the muscles in the back of your throat. (5 repetitions, 3-5 times a day)
08-06-07.heading: Exercise #2: Tongue Hold (Masako)

chunks:
Exercise #3: Effortful Swallow
1. Swallow with extra force 2. Feel your tongue against the roof of your mouth as you swallow (5 repetitions, 3-5 times a day)
08-06-08.heading: Exercise #3: Effortful Swallow

chunks:
Exercise #4: Tongue Pull-back
1. Say the “k-k-k-k-k” harshly 2. Feel the engagement of the back of the tongue (5 repetitions, 3-5 times a day)
08-06-09.heading: Exercise #4: Tongue Pull-back

chunks:
Exercise #5: Pharyngeal Constriction
1. Say a high pitched “ee” sound for 5 seconds 2. Watch yourself in the mirror and make sure your neck muscles are engaged (5 repetitions, 3-5 times a day)
08-06-10.heading: Exercise #5: Pharyngeal Constriction

chunks:
Exercise #6: Mendelsohn Maneuver
1. Feel the top of your larynx (Adam’s apple) moving upward during a swallow 2. At the highest point of your swallow (when you hear the clicking sound), try to hold the larynx up. 3. Hold your breath for 5 seconds.
This exercise helps lift your larynx and opens the top of your food pipe (esophagus). This can help clear out any leftover food stuck in your throat. (5 repetitions, 3-5 times a day)
08-06-11.heading: Exercise #6: Mendelsohn Maneuver

chunks:
When are these exercises useful?
Helpful for:
• Laryngectomy (partial or total)
• Oropharynx surgery
• Radiation to throat or neck Beneﬁts:
• Keeps swallowing muscles strong
• Speeds up recovery after treatment
• Lowers risk of feeding tube or aspiration
• Helps you keep eating by mouth longer
08-06-12.heading: When are these exercises useful?

Exercises
08-06-13.heading: Spinal Accessory Nerve

chunks:
What is the spinal accessory nerve?
The spinal accessory nerve is located in the back of your upper shoulder. When the nerve is injured, it can cause pain and can greatly reduce the range of motion in that shoulder
08-06-14.heading: What is the spinal accessory nerve?

chunks:
Exercise #1: Shoulder Shrugs
1. Shoulder shrugs can strengthen the injured area. 2. Stand with your legs hip-distance apart. 3. Shrug your shoulders up and lower them down as far as you comfortably can 4. Do a total of 10 repetitions 5. As you progress hold weights in your hands as you do this exercise
08-06-15.heading: Exercise #1: Shoulder Shrugs

chunks:
Exercise #2: Supine Shoulder Rotation
1. Use a bed or mat for another strengthening exercise 2. Lie on your back and bend your elbows 3. Your upper arm should be at your side horizontal to the ground and your lower arms in the air perpendicular to the ground 4. Slowly bring your hands down to the mat or bed and back up in the air 5. Do a total of 10 repetitions
08-06-16.heading: Exercise #2: Supine Shoulder Rotation

chunks:
Exercise #3: Shoulder Elevation with Wand
1. The American Physical Therapy Association suggests this exercise that involves using a cane, broomstick or dowel 2. Lie on your back holding the cane, broomstick or dowel with your hands resting on your upper legs 3. Your hands should be about 18 inches apart, and your palms should be facing up 4. Slowly lift your arms as far over your head as is comfortable, leading with the uninjured arm 5. Hold for 5 seconds and return to your original position do a total of ﬁve repetitions
08-06-17.heading: Exercise #3: Shoulder Elevation with Wand

chunks:
Exercise #4: Wall Slide
1. The APTA also recommends a standing exercise to rehabilitate a spinal accessory nerve injury 2. Stand close to a wall, facing sideways 3. Slide your injured arm up the wall using your ﬁngers to walk up the wall, palms facing down 4. Keep sliding your hand until you feel a stretch and hold the position for 5 seconds 5. Slowly drop your arm and do a total of ﬁve repetitions 6. Do not make the mistake of turning your body towards the wall
08-06-18.heading: Exercise #4: Wall Slide

chunks:
Exercise #5: Wall Press
1. Stand facing a wall for this strengthening exercise 2. You should be two to three feet away from the wall 3. Put your hands on the wall at shoulder level and press against it 4. As you do this, squeeze your shoulder blades together and then separate them 5. Return to your starting position 6. Do a total of 10 repetitions
08-06-19.heading: Exercise #5: Wall Press

chunks:
When are these exercises useful?
Helpful for: Neck dissection surgery (especially levels II–V) Beneﬁts:
• Protects shoulder and neck strength
• Reduces risk of shoulder pain and stiffness
• Improves posture and range of motion
• Easier return to normal activity after surgery
08-06-20.heading: When are these exercises useful?

chunks:
Why do I need radiation after surgery?
You may need radiation after surgery based on certain risk features found in your tumor. Radiation is used to reduce the risk of cancer returning after surgery.
When cancer comes back after treatment, it's called a recurrence. Radiation helps lower the chances of this happening.
09-01-04.heading: Why do I need radiation after surgery?

chunks:
Common Reasons for Postoperative Radiation
• Advanced stage primary tumor: If your tumor is classiﬁed as T3 or T4 (larger or more invasive tumors), radiation is typically recommended.
• Perineural invasion: If cancer is found spreading along small nerves, this increases the risk of recurrence.
• Lymphovascular invasion: Cancer cells found in small blood vessels or lymphatic vessels suggest a higher likelihood of spread.
09-01-05.heading: Common Reasons for Postoperative Radiation

chunks:
Common Reasons for Postoperative Radiation (cont.)
• Close margins: If the tumor is close to the edge of the surgical specimen, there may be microscopic cancer left behind.
• Lymph node involvement:
○ Multiple lymph nodes with cancer (pathologic N2 or N3 disease) ○ Large lymph nodes involved ○ Involvement of low or posterior neck lymph nodes (levels 4 or 5)
09-01-06.heading: Common Reasons for Postoperative Radiation (cont.)

chunks:
What is chemotherapy?
Chemotherapy is medicine that travels through your whole body to kill cancer cells. It’s usually given by IV or as a pill, and it works by targeting fast-growing cells like cancer.
09-01-08.heading: What is chemotherapy?

chunks:
Why do I need both radiation and chemotherapy after surgery?
In some cases, chemotherapy is added to radiation therapy to improve treatment outcomes. This decision is based on certain high-risk features found during surgery.
This combination of treatments may increase side effects but can improve the chances of cure in high-risk patients.
09-01-09.heading: Why do I need both radiation and chemotherapy after surgery?

chunks:
Common Reasons for Postoperative Radiation with Chemotherapy
• Positive surgical margins: If cancer cells are seen right at the edge of the removed tissue, this indicates that not all cancer may have been removed.
• Extracapsular spread (ECS): If cancer has spread outside a lymph node into surrounding tissue, chemotherapy is typically recommended in addition to radiation.

09-01-11.heading: Timing of Postoperative

chunks:
When do I start receiving postoperative radiation therapy?
Radiation is most effective when started soon after surgery, once you have healed but before too much time passes.
09-01-12.heading: When do I start receiving postoperative radiation therapy?

chunks:
What is a typical timeline?
• Start radiation within 6 weeks of surgery, ideally.
• This allows enough time for surgical healing while ensuring radiation is still effective.
• Delays beyond 8 weeks may reduce treatment success, so it's important to keep appointments and complete pre-radiation evaluations on time.

chunks:
Why do I need to see the dentist?
Radiation to the head and neck can damage your salivary glands and cause xerostomia (dry mouth) which increases the risk of:
• Cavities and dental infections
• Osteoradionecrosis (jawbone damage)
• Other long-term dental complications
09-02-04.heading: Why do I need to see the dentist?

chunks:
What do I need to do?
• Schedule a pre-radiation dental evaluation at least a few weeks before starting radiation.
• Your dentist will check for and treat any dental issues beforehand.
• You may need extractions, ﬁllings, or cleanings to reduce the risk of problems during or after treatment.
09-02-05.heading: What do I need to do?

chunks:
Goals of Pre-Radiation Oral/Dental Evaluation:
• Patient education (both oral and written) about dental risks and preventive care
• Complete head and neck dental exam, including x-rays
• Identify and treat sources of infection before radiation
09-02-06.heading: Goals of Pre-Radiation Oral/Dental Evaluation:

chunks:
Dry Mouth Management
• Increase hydration
• Avoid caffeine and alcohol
• Use salivary stimulants (e.g., xylitol gum/lozenges, sorbitol, pilocarpine, cevimeline)
• Use alcohol-free mouthwash (e.g., 0.1% chlorine dioxide rinse)
• Use salivary substitutes (e.g., gels with lysozyme, lactoferrin, calcium phosphate)
09-02-08.heading: Dry Mouth Management

chunks:
Dental Caries Prevention
• Brush and ﬂoss daily
• Use ﬂuoride treatments: ○ 1.1% NaF gel or dentifrice daily ○ Fluoride varnish 3x/year ○ Calcium phosphate rinses/gels
• Frequent dental checkups
09-02-09.heading: Dental Caries Prevention

chunks:
Fungal Infection Prevention
• Antifungal lozenges or rinses
• Systemic antifungals if needed (consult infectious disease specialist)
09-02-10.heading: Fungal Infection Prevention

chunks:
Extractions and Jaw Tightness
• Determine if tooth extractions are needed before RT (at least 2 weeks prior)
• Coordinate any future extractions with your oncology team
• Monitor and manage trismus (jaw tightness)
09-02-11.heading: Extractions and Jaw Tightness

chunks:
Post-Treatment Dental Management
• Continue managing dry mouth and trismus
• Maintain strict oral hygiene and caries prevention
• Prevent/manage osteoradionecrosis
• Avoid implants or extractions without radiation oncologist consultation
• Dental visits every 6 months or more frequently if xerostomia or new dental issues arise

10-01-03.heading: Health Promotion and

chunks:
Recommendations for survivors post-treatment
• Maintain a healthy weight and eat healthy, focusing on eating vegetables, fruits, and whole grains
• Adopt a physically active lifestyle, including exercise and strength training as tolerated
• We strongly recommend quitting tobacco and limiting alcohol intake
• Visit the dentist at least once a year
• Use at least SPF 30 sunscreen daily
• Notify your doctor of any family history of cancer
10-01-04.heading: Recommendations for survivors post-treatment

chunks:
What action steps can be taken towards wellness?
• If food intake is an issue or if there are feeding tube issues, notify your doctor
• Always consult your doctor before starting an exercise program
• Tobacco cessation counseling is available if you need assistance
• If you notice any oral cavity changes, notify your doctor
10-01-05.heading: What action steps can be taken towards wellness?

chunks:
Patients should continue to be mindful of
• Follow-up visits:

○ Year 1: every 1-3 months ○ Year 2: every 2-6 months ○ Years 3-5: every 4-8 months ○ Years 6+: every 12 months
• Imaging: a CT scan, MRI, or PET may be ordered 3 months post-treatment
• Thyroid function: Evaluate function every 6-12 months for 6 years post-treatment
• Vaccinations: Stay up to date with your inﬂuenza, shingles, and pneumococcal vaccines

10-01-08.heading: Screening for Secondary

chunks:
How are second primary cancers detected?
• Head and neck cancer survivors are at increased risk for new head and neck, lung, and esophageal cancers
• The risk of developing these can vary depending on treatment variations, age, and genetics
• Your doctor may decide to screen for lung cancer with CT scans
• All other cancers can be screened for as they normally are
